words.en: 1) to explain why something happens; 2) to make up a part or amount of something
words.usage: account for + phenomenon (account for the persistence of X); X accounts for 30% of Y; fail to account for + case
words.ety: Old French aconter (to count up), from Latin computare; cf. count, compute, accountability
words.tip: Give an account of it = tell the story of how it came about. A good theory accounts for the data: every case gets an explanation.
ex: Butler's theory struggles to account for why some slurs lose their power over time.

words.en: to make something clear by explaining it; to shed light on
words.usage: elucidate + concept / relationship / meaning; elucidate how / why + clause; elucidation (n.); serve to elucidate
words.ety: Latin e- (out) + lucidus (bright, clear), from lux (light); cf. lucid, translucent, illuminate
words.tip: lux = light. To elucidate is to bring a dark idea out into the light. ⚠ explicate = unfold what is implied; elucidate = make what's obscure clear.
ex: This chapter seeks to elucidate the relationship between speech acts and social harm.

words.en: to explain in detail by unfolding what is implied
words.usage: explicate an idea / a concept; explicate what X means
words.ety: Latin ex- (out) + plicare (to fold): to unfold
words.tip: Same root as implicit / explicit. Explicating turns the implicit into the explicit.
words.text: "such an attempt to explicate these ideas would invariably result in the unveiling of nuances of meaning"
ex: Chapter 2 explicates Butler's notion of linguistic vulnerability.

words.en: intended to explain or describe something clearly (rather than to tell a story or persuade)
words.ko: 설명적인, 해설하는; expository writing = 설명문; exposition = 해설, 상세한 설명
words.usage: expository writing / essay / text / prose; largely / purely expository; expository vs. narrative / persuasive / descriptive; an exposition of + theory
words.ety: Latin ex- (out) + ponere (to put, place), via expositus; cf. expose, expound, exposition, expo, position
words.tip: ex- + ponere = put out → lay your ideas out on the table for everyone to see. Same root as expose, expound, and expo. In papers, 'this section is expository' = 'here I explain others' views; my own argument comes later.' ⚠ expository vs. exploratory (탐색적인).
ex: My son's homework this week is to write a short expository essay on how volcanoes form.
The museum's labels are expository, explaining each painting's history in plain language.
Most news reports are meant to be expository rather than persuasive.
Fourth graders often find expository texts harder to read than stories.
The first half of the paper is expository, laying out Austin's speech act theory before applying it to hate speech.

words.en: unclear, vague, imprecise
words.usage: fuzzy thinking; a fuzzy concept / distinction
words.ety: Origin uncertain; literally fluffy or blurred
words.tip: Picture a blurry, out-of-focus photo. Its opposite in Ch. 3 is the analysts' favorite word, clarity.
words.text: "Analytic philosophers accused traditional philosophers of fuzzy thinking"
ex: The policy relies on fuzzy terms like "respect" without defining them.

words.en: strictness and precision in thinking or method; careful exactness
words.usage: with rigor; methodological / conceptual rigor; a rigorous argument / analysis
words.ety: Latin rigor (stiffness); cf. rigid, rigor mortis
words.tip: Rigorous thinking is stiff and doesn't bend or wobble, like something rigid.
words.text: "find ways to analyze, or at least discuss with some rigor, the full range of human concerns"
ex: The paper lacks conceptual rigor in defining "harm."

words.en: easy to see or notice; standing out (sometimes in an unwanted way)
words.usage: conspicuous + noun (a conspicuous absence / sign / omission); be conspicuous by its absence (없어서 오히려 눈에 띄다); conspicuous consumption (과시적 소비); make oneself conspicuous; inconspicuous = 눈에 안 띄는
words.ety: Latin con- (intensive) + specere 'to look' → 'clearly visible'. Same root: inspect, spectacle, perspective, suspicious
words.tip: spec = look (spectacle, inspect) → con-SPIC-uous = 'everyone's eyes land on it.' ⚠ conspicuous (눈에 띄는) vs. inconspicuous (눈에 안 띄는) — not 'conscious'
ex: She wore a bright red coat, so she was conspicuous in the crowd.
The cat's food bowl was in a conspicuous spot by the door.
Put the warning sign in a conspicuous place so everyone can see it.
Veblen coined the term 'conspicuous consumption' to describe buying luxury goods to display status.
Students' own languages are conspicuously absent from the school's official curriculum.

words.en: essential to a whole; a necessary part that cannot be removed without changing the whole
words.ko: 필수적인, 없어서는 안 될, (전체를 이루는) 핵심적인
words.usage: an integral part / component / element of X; integral to + noun (integral to the plan); become an integral part of X
words.ety: Latin integer (whole, untouched); cf. integer, integrity, integrate, entire
words.tip: integer = whole. An integral part is a piece the whole needs to stay whole. ⚠ integral (필수적인 일부) ≠ integrated (통합된) ≠ integrative (통합적인).
words.text: "[the Protocols] were used to justify the massacres of Jews during the Russian Civil War and became an integral part of Nazi ideology."
ex: Rice is an integral part of most Korean meals.
Teamwork is integral to the success of any project.
Music became an integral part of her daily routine.
Critical thinking is an integral component of the new curriculum.
For Butler, the history of a slur's use is integral to its power to wound.

words.en: most noticeable or important; standing out from the rest and drawing attention
words.ko: 두드러진, 눈에 띄는, 가장 중요한, 핵심적인
words.usage: a salient feature / point / fact / issue / difference; the most salient aspect; salient to + person or context; make X salient; become salient; salience (n.)
words.ety: Latin salire (to leap); cf. result, assault, sally, somersault
words.tip: salient = leaping out at you. salire (leap) also gives result (leaps back) and assault (leaps at). A salient point jumps out of the text. Note: it means 'stands out', so it can differ from 'important', and in philosophy/psychology 'make X salient' means bring X to attention.
ex: The most salient feature of the town is its enormous clock tower.
Let me summarize the salient points of the meeting for those who missed it.
After the accident, safety became a salient concern for the whole family.
In a classroom of mostly white students, her race was salient to her in ways it wasn't elsewhere.
A good abstract states the question and the salient findings, not every detail.

words.en: (n.) the main point or direction of an argument; a strong push. (v.) to push suddenly and forcefully; to force someone into a situation
words.ko: (n.) 요지, 핵심, 취지; 밀침 (v.) 확 밀다, 밀어 넣다, (상황에) 떠밀다
words.usage: the (main/central) thrust of + argument/paper/policy; thrust something into/at something; be thrust into (a role / the spotlight); thrust upon someone
words.ety: Old Norse þrysta 'to press, compress'. Related: thrusting, (engine) thrust
words.tip: Picture a spear thrust forward: the thrust of an argument is the direction the whole argument pushes toward. Main thrust ≈ gist / main point / upshot
words.text: "Freud happened on a developmental thrust within the individual toward a rational orientation to the world." (here: an inner drive/push in development, 발달적 추동력)
ex: He thrust his hands into his pockets to keep them warm.
She was thrust into the spotlight after her video went viral.
Many new teachers are thrust into leadership roles before they feel ready.
The main thrust of the policy is to reduce class sizes.
The central thrust of Butler's argument is that injurious speech can be resignified rather than simply censored.

words.en: v. to express an idea or feeling clearly in words; adj. able to express oneself clearly and well
words.ko: v. (생각을) 분명하게 표현하다, 명료하게 말로 풀어내다 / adj. (말을) 조리 있게 잘하는
words.usage: v. articulate + idea / concern / position / vision; articulate what / how + clause; adj. an articulate speaker / student; articulation (n.); inarticulate (adj.)
words.ety: Latin articulus (small joint), from artus (joint); cf. article, arthritis
words.tip: A joint divides a limb into clear, connected parts. To articulate an idea is to put it into clearly jointed words. ⚠ vs. eloquent: articulate = clear; eloquent = clear AND moving/beautiful.
ex: She was too upset to articulate what was wrong.
He's a very articulate kid; he explains his reasons better than most adults.
Can you articulate exactly what you want from this job?
Many students feel hurt by a slur but struggle to articulate why it wounds.
This paper articulates a theory of linguistic injury that draws on Austin and Butler.

words.en: adj. fluent, expressive, and persuasive in speaking or writing; also (of a look or gesture) vividly expressive without words
words.ko: adj. 유창하고 설득력 있는, 웅변의 / n. 웅변, 능변, 유려한 표현력
words.usage: an eloquent speech / speaker / plea / defense of X; speak eloquently about X; an eloquent silence / look; eloquence (n.)
words.ety: Latin e- (out) + loqui (to speak); cf. loquacious, colloquial, soliloquy, interlocutor
words.tip: e-loqui = speaking out, beautifully. Same root as colloquial (speaking together) and interlocutor (one who speaks between). ⚠ Higher than articulate: eloquent speech moves people, not just informs them.
words.text: "The secret to eloquence" (back cover)
ex: Her eloquent speech at the funeral left everyone in tears.
He isn't eloquent, but he's honest, and people trust him.
The child's silence was more eloquent than any apology.
King's letter is an eloquent defense of nonviolent resistance.
Butler writes eloquently about how being named can both wound and constitute the subject.

words.en: having many small parts or details that fit together in a complicated way; very detailed and complex
words.usage: an intricate pattern / design / plot / argument / relationship; intricately carved / connected / woven; intricacy (n.), the intricacies of X
words.ety: Latin intricare (to entangle), in- (in) + tricae (tricks, perplexities, tangles); cf. extricate (to untangle, get out of)
words.tip: in + tricae = 'tangled in.' Its opposite-direction cousin is extricate (to pull out of a tangle). ⚠ vs. complicated: complicated often = hard and annoying; intricate = complex but finely made, often admired.
ex: Her sweater has an intricate pattern of tiny snowflakes.
The novel's plot is so intricate that I had to draw a chart of the characters.
Watchmakers spend years learning to assemble such intricate mechanisms.
Learning a new language means slowly mastering the intricacies of its grammar.
Butler traces the intricate relationship between being named, being injured, and becoming a subject.

words.en: n. (1) a trial period in which someone (a new employee, member, student) must prove they are suitable; (2) a legal sentence letting an offender stay out of prison under supervision; (3) academic probation: a warning status for students whose grades fall too low
words.ko: n. 수습 기간, 시험 채용 기간; (법) 보호관찰; (학업) 학사경고
words.usage: on probation; put / place someone on probation; a probation period; sentenced to X years' probation; academic probation; probation officer; probationary (adj.): a probationary period / teacher; probationer (n.)
words.ety: Latin probatio (a test, proof), from probare (to test, prove); cf. prove, probe, probable, approbation
words.tip: Probation = a "prove-ation": a period when you must PROVE yourself. Same root as probe (to test) and prove.
ex: New hires are on probation for the first three months.
He was sentenced to two years' probation instead of jail time.
If your GPA drops below 3.0, you'll be placed on academic probation.
The club let him back in, but only on probation: one more fight and he's out.
The university placed the program on probation after it failed to meet accreditation standards.

words.en: a person who helps another to do something wrong or illegal
words.ko: 공범, 공모자; complicit = 연루된, 가담한; complicity = 공모, 가담
words.usage: an accomplice to / in + crime; act as an accomplice; an unwitting accomplice; be complicit in + noun; complicity in + noun
words.ety: Latin complex, complicis (closely connected), from com- (together) + plicare (to fold); Middle English 'a complice' → accomplice; cf. complicit, complicated, implicate
words.tip: com + plicare = folded together → someone tangled up with the main wrongdoer. Same plic- as complicated and complicit. ⚠ accomplice (공범) vs. accomplish (성취하다): different roots.
ex: My little brother was my accomplice in sneaking cookies before dinner.
The driver of the getaway car was charged as an accomplice.
Police arrested the hacker and two accomplices.
A teacher who laughs along with a cruel joke can become an unwitting accomplice to bullying.
Some theorists argue that institutions that tolerate slurs act as accomplices, lending the speaker their authority.

words.en: v. (of a court or jury) to officially declare someone not guilty of a crime; (idiom) acquit oneself well = to perform or behave well
words.ko: v. 무죄를 선고하다, 무죄 방면하다 / n. acquittal: 무죄 선고 / acquit oneself well: (일을) 잘 해내다
words.usage: acquit someone of + charge (acquitted of murder); be acquitted; win an acquittal; acquit oneself well / admirably; ⚠ opposite of convict (유죄 판결하다), nearly opposite of incriminate (죄를 씌우다)
words.ety: Old French aquiter (to settle, free), from Latin ad- (to) + quietare (to make quiet, settle); cf. quit, quiet
words.tip: ac-QUIT: the court lets you QUIT the charge, and you go free and quiet. ⚠ incriminate = makes you look guilty; acquit = the court says 'not guilty.'
ex: The jury acquitted him after only two hours of deliberation.
She was acquitted of all charges.
Despite the acquittal, many people still believed he was guilty.
The new DNA evidence led to his acquittal.
Being acquitted in court does not erase the social harm of being publicly accused.

words.en: a secret plan by two or more people to do something illegal or harmful; (law) the crime of agreeing to commit a crime
words.usage: conspiracy to + verb (conspiracy to commit fraud); a conspiracy against X; uncover / expose a conspiracy; conspire with someone to do X; a conspiracy of silence
words.ety: Latin con- (together) + spirare (to breathe): 'breathe together'; cf. inspire, respiration, expire, spirit
words.tip: Breathe together': heads so close that their breath mixes while they whisper a secret plan. Cassam's three parts: a small group + in secret + illegal or harmful.
words.text: "A conspiracy requires a small group of conspirators who work together in secret to do something illegal or harmful."
ex: The two brothers were found guilty of conspiracy to commit fraud.
Police uncovered a conspiracy to rob the bank.
There was a conspiracy of silence about the abuse in the team.
The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 was a real conspiracy to blow up Parliament.
Calling every coordinated act of resistance a "conspiracy" can be a way to delegitimize political protest.

words.en: n. the act of making something no longer a criminal offense (it may still be regulated or fined)
words.usage: the decriminalization of X; decriminalize drug possession / sex work; ⚠ vs. legalization: decriminalized = no criminal penalty but possibly fines; legalized = fully permitted and regulated; opposite: criminalization / criminalize
words.ety: Latin de- (away, remove) + crimen (charge) + -al + -ize + -ation
words.tip: de + crim = take the crime label AWAY. Not 'allowed' (legalized), just 'no longer a crime.'
ex: Some cities have moved toward the decriminalization of jaywalking.
Portugal is known for decriminalizing personal drug possession in 2001.
Decriminalization is not the same as legalization: you may still pay a fine.
Activists campaigned for the decriminalization of homosexuality in countries where it was still a crime.
Debates over hate speech regulation often ask whether criminalization or decriminalization better protects targeted groups.

words.en: v. to make someone appear guilty of a crime or wrongdoing; to provide evidence of guilt
words.ko: v. 죄를 씌우다, 유죄로 보이게 하다 / incriminating: 유죄를 입증하는 / self-incrimination: 자기부죄
words.usage: incriminate oneself; incriminating evidence / messages / documents; self-incrimination; the right against self-incrimination
words.ety: Latin in- (into) + crimen (charge, accusation); cf. crime, criminal, recrimination, decriminalize
words.tip: in + crim = put the charge INTO someone: you load the crime onto them.
ex: The suspect refused to answer, fearing he might incriminate himself.
Police found incriminating text messages on her phone.
He tried to incriminate his coworker by hiding the money in her desk.
The Fifth Amendment protects people from being forced to incriminate themselves.
Students may stay silent about online harassment if speaking up would incriminate their friends.

words.en: n. an accusation made in response to someone else's accusation; mutual blaming (often plural)
words.usage: bitter / mutual recriminations; dissolve into recriminations; without recrimination; recriminate (v., rare)
words.ety: Latin re- (back) + criminari (to accuse), from crimen; cf. crime, incriminate
words.tip: re + crim = throw the charge BACK. You blame me, I blame you back, and that's recrimination.
ex: After the breakup, there were no tears, only bitter recriminations.
The meeting dissolved into mutual recriminations over who missed the deadline.
Let's fix the problem instead of wasting time on recriminations.
After the election loss, the party was consumed by recrimination.
Restorative approaches aim to move a school community beyond blame and recrimination toward repair.

words.en: n. the legal process of proving that a dead person's will is valid and distributing their property (estate); v. (US) to prove a will officially
words.usage: go through probate; avoid probate; probate court; probate lawyer; the will was probated / admitted to probate; ⚠ not the same as probation
words.ety: Latin probatum (a thing proved), from probare (to test, prove); cf. probation, prove, probe
words.tip: probate = PROVE the will; probation = PROVE yourself. Same root, different 'test.'
ex: After her grandfather died, the family had to wait months for probate to finish.
The house can't be sold until the will goes through probate.
Many Americans set up a living trust to avoid probate.
A probate court ruled that the handwritten will was valid.
Probate disputes often show how family conflict gets translated into legal language.

words.en: to block something so that it builds up behind a barrier; (fig.) to hold back feelings or energy until pressure builds
words.usage: dam up + water / feelings / energy; dammed-up emotion / anger; be dammed up
words.ety: Old English/Middle Dutch dam (barrier holding back water)
words.tip: Picture a beaver's dam: the water piles up behind it until it finds another way out. Freud pictured feelings the same way: blocked feelings build pressure and leak out as symptoms.
words.text: Hysterical symptoms are supposedly generated by damming up psychical energy which is then channeled into causing a somatic symptom.
words.source: Lear, Love and Its Place in Nature, Ch. 2, p. 44
ex: Beavers dam up the stream to make a pond.
Fallen trees dammed up the river after the storm.
She had dammed up her anger for years, and one day it all came out.
In Freud's early theory, psychical energy that is dammed up finds release in a bodily symptom.
Lear questions whether emotion is really something that can be dammed up like water.

words.en: the spending or using up of money, energy, time, or effort
words.usage: expenditure of energy / effort / time; public / government expenditure; expend (v.)
words.ety: Latin expendere (to weigh out, pay out), ex- (out) + pendere (to weigh, pay); cf. spend, expense, pension
words.tip: ex + pend = weigh out coins to pay. Spend is a shortened form of the same word. In Freud's energy model, keeping a symptom going costs energy, so it is an expenditure.
words.source: Lear, Love and Its Place in Nature, Ch. 2 (around p. 44)
ex: Government expenditure on education rose this year.
We need to cut our monthly expenditure on eating out.
Moving all those boxes was a huge expenditure of energy.
On Freud's model, maintaining a symptom requires a continuous expenditure of psychical energy.
Lear asks why, if symptoms cost energy, they don't simply die out on their own.

words.en: choked off; blocked from flowing out or being expressed
words.usage: strangulated emotion / affect / voice / cry; a strangulated hernia (medical); strangle (v.); strangulation (n.)
words.ety: Latin strangulare (to choke), from Greek strangalē (halter, cord); cf. strangle, string, strict, constrain
words.tip: A strangulated emotion has been 'strangled' before it could speak, like a throat squeezed shut. ⚠ Stronger and more physical than stifled (억눌러 참은).
words.text: "Freud and Breuer referred to it as 'strangulated emotion.'"
words.source: Lear, Love and Its Place in Nature, Ch. 2, p. 41
ex: The cat let out a strangulated meow when it got stuck behind the sofa.
She answered in a strangulated voice, trying not to cry.
In medicine, a strangulated hernia has its blood supply cut off and needs urgent surgery.
Freud and Breuer described the trauma's affect as strangulated: never expressed, so it found an outlet in the body.
Hate speech can leave a strangulated response in its targets, an anger that has no safe place to be spoken.

words.en: 1) a change from one form, use, or belief to another; 2) (psychoanalysis) the turning of mental distress into a physical symptom
words.ko: 1) 전환, 변환, 개종; 2) (정신분석) 전환: 마음의 고통이 몸의 증상으로 바뀌는 것
words.usage: conversion of A into B; convert A into B; conversion hysteria / conversion disorder; religious conversion
words.ety: Latin convertere (to turn around), con- (completely) + vertere (to turn); cf. convert, reverse, divert, version
words.tip: con + vert = turn completely around. Mental pain turns around and comes out as bodily pain. ⚠ Lear: at the archaic level no 'leap' from mind to body is needed, because the body is the mind.
words.text: "A hysterical symptom, Freud thought, represented the conversion of something mental into something physical."
words.source: Lear, Love and Its Place in Nature, Ch. 2, p. 39
ex: The bank charges a fee for currency conversion from dollars to won.
The old factory's conversion into apartments took two years.
His conversion to Buddhism surprised his family.
Freud saw Elisabeth von R.'s leg pain as the conversion of mental pain into physical pain.
Lear argues that the idea of conversion assumes a gap between mind and body that archaic mind does not have.

words.en: to make someone believe something that is not true
words.ko: 속이다; deception, deceit = 속임, 기만 (deceive oneself = 자기기만하다)
words.usage: deceive someone (into doing something); deceive oneself; be deceived by + noun; an act of deception; deceptive (adj.)
words.ety: Latin de- (away, from) + capere (to take); cf. conceive, perceive, receive; deceptive, self-deception
words.tip: de- = away → take the truth away from someone. ⚠ deceive (속이다) vs. receive (받다): de- takes away, re- takes back to yourself.
ex: Don't be deceived by his friendly smile.
The ad deceived customers into thinking the product was free.
She deceived herself into believing the relationship would get better.
Researchers must not deceive participants about the risks of a study.
Propaganda works by deceiving people while appearing to inform them.

words.en: believing something false despite clear evidence; fooled, often by oneself
words.usage: a deluded + person (a deluded Conspiracy Theorist); be deluded into thinking that + clause; delude oneself (that ...); under the delusion that ...; delusions of grandeur
words.ety: Latin de- (down, away) + ludere (to play): 'play someone false, mock'; cf. illusion, ludicrous, elude, interlude
words.tip: ludere = play. A deluded person has been played: by others or by their own mind. ⚠ deluded (망상에 빠진, sincerely wrong) vs. deceived (속은, tricked by someone else) vs. dishonest (알면서 거짓말).
words.text: "The deluded Sandy Hook Conspiracy Theorist who sincerely believes that the whole thing was a hoax will be no less effective ..."
ex: He's deluded if he thinks he can pass without studying.
Don't delude yourself; she isn't coming back.
The patient was under the delusion that someone was following him.
The CEO was deluded into thinking the product would sell itself.
A speaker may be deluded rather than malicious, yet his words can still do real harm to the people they target.

words.en: severe mental or emotional suffering
words.usage: in anguish; cry out in anguish; the anguish of + noun (loss, separation); mental / emotional anguish; an anguished cry / face
words.ety: Latin angustia (narrowness, tightness), from angere (to squeeze, choke); cf. anxiety, anxious, angina
words.tip: angere = to squeeze → a pain that tightens your chest until you can hardly breathe. Same root as anxiety (both feel 'tight'). ⚠ pain = broad (body or mind); anguish = intense, mostly emotional.
ex: She cried out in anguish when she heard the news.
His face was twisted with anguish as he waited outside the hospital room.
The families of the missing passengers spent days in anguish.
The child's anguished drawings revealed what she could not put into words.
Victims of hate speech often describe a lasting anguish that the law fails to recognize as harm.

words.en: sad and lonely because abandoned or left alone; (of hope or an attempt) unlikely to succeed
words.ko: 쓸쓸한, 버림받은 듯 처량한; forlornness = 쓸쓸함, 처량함; forlorn hope = 헛된 희망
words.usage: look / feel / stand forlorn; a forlorn figure / place; a forlorn hope; the forlornness of + noun
words.ety: Old English forloren (utterly lost), past participle of forleosan: for- (completely) + leosan (to lose); cf. German verloren, lose, lost
words.tip: for-lorn = for-lost → completely lost, left behind with nothing. Stronger than lonely: abandoned and visibly pitiful. ⚠ Spelling: for-LORN (not 'folorn').
ex: A forlorn puppy sat in the rain outside the shop.
After the guests left, the house felt forlorn and too quiet.
Waiting for a ceasefire had become a forlorn hope for the villagers.
The new student stood forlorn at the edge of the playground, unsure whom to approach.
The forlornness of being repeatedly named as an outsider can leave a child feeling she has no place in the class.

words.en: the state of being completely absorbed; (Noddings) the carer's receptive attention to the cared-for's reality
words.ko: 몰입, 전념, (상대에게) 온전히 빠져듦; be engrossed in = ~에 몰두하다; (Noddings) 수용적 몰입
words.usage: be engrossed in + noun/-ing; in (total) engrossment; (Noddings) engrossment and motivational displacement; the one-caring's engrossment in the cared-for
words.ety: Old French en gros (in bulk, wholesale): en- (in) + gros (large, whole); cf. gross, grocer
words.tip: en + gros = taken in whole → pulled entirely into something. Noddings: engrossment (receive the other's reality) + motivational displacement (my energy flows toward their needs) = the core of caring.
ex: She was so engrossed in her book that she missed her bus stop.
The kids sat in total engrossment as the magician performed.
Viewers' engrossment in their phones has changed how people behave in public spaces.
For Noddings, a teacher's engrossment means receiving what the student is actually feeling, not what the lesson plan expects.
Responding well to a student hurt by a slur begins with engrossment: listening to how the word landed for her before explaining why it was wrong.

words.en: (psychoanalysis) to release a repressed emotion by reliving and expressing the experience that caused it
words.usage: abreact + an emotion / a trauma / an affect; abreaction (n.); achieve / bring about abreaction; abreactive (adj.)
words.ety: German abreagieren (Breuer & Freud): ab- 'off, away' + reagieren 'react'; cf. react, reaction, catharsis
words.tip: ab- = off/away: you 'react it off' — the reaction that was stuck finally gets discharged. ⚠ The opposite of 'strangulated' emotion: abreaction is what un-strangles it.
ex: After the accident, talking it through with friends helped him abreact some of the shock.
Crying at the funeral let her abreact the grief she had been holding in.
In early talk therapy, patients abreacted old traumas by recounting them in detail.
Breuer and Freud believed that hysterical symptoms disappeared once the strangulated affect was abreacted.
Lear questions whether abreaction alone can explain the cure, since it treats emotion like a fluid to be drained.

words.en: n. a large and impressive range of things; v. to arrange in order
words.ko: (다양한 것들의) 집합, 다수, 배열; v. 배열하다, 늘어세우다; disarray = 혼란, 흐트러짐
words.usage: a (wide / vast / diverse / dazzling) array of + plural noun; array X across / along Y; in disarray
words.ety: Old French areer (to arrange), from Latin ad- (to) + Germanic *raid- (ready, ordered); cf. ready, disarray
words.tip: array = things lined up neatly on display (a shop shelf); disarray = the lines knocked out of order. 'an array of' ≈ 'a range of', but with a picture of things spread out before you.
ex: The bakery offers a dazzling array of breads and pastries.
She arrayed her photos neatly across the table.
The city faces an array of problems, from housing costs to traffic.
Teachers draw on a wide array of strategies to support multilingual learners.
Hate speech takes an array of forms, from explicit slurs to coded jokes and images.

words.en: pure, nothing but; used before a noun to stress how great something is
words.usage: sheer + noun: sheer force / luck / size / number / volume / will(power) / joy; by sheer chance
words.ety: Old English scīr (bright, pure, clear); cf. German schier (pure, almost)
words.tip: Sheer fabric is thin and see-through: pure, nothing mixed in. Sheer luck = pure luck, nothing else. ⚠ a sheer cliff = a straight-down drop (separate meaning).
words.text: "one should not underestimate the sheer force of the pressure, both physical and mental, which Freud exerted on his patients"
words.source: Lear, Love and Its Place in Nature, Ch. 2, p. 59
ex: We won by sheer luck. Nobody actually played well.
The sheer size of the library made me feel lost on my first day.
She finished the marathon through sheer willpower.
The sheer volume of hate speech online makes case-by-case moderation nearly impossible.
Lear warns against underestimating the sheer pressure Freud put on his patients.

words.en: angry, bitter, and hostile (of an argument or relationship)
words.usage: an acrimonious debate / dispute; become acrimonious
words.ety: Latin acer (sharp, sour); cf. acid, acrid
words.tip: An acrimonious argument leaves a sour, acidic taste.
words.text: "The argument between traditional philosophers of education and analytic philosophers sometimes became acrimonious."
ex: The faculty meeting turned acrimonious over the new grading policy.

words.en: disputed; actively argued over, with no agreed answer
words.usage: a contested concept / term / claim; highly / deeply contested; essentially contested concept (Gallie)
words.ety: Latin contestari (to call to witness), con- (together) + testis (witness); cf. testify, protest
words.tip: A contest has rival sides. A contested concept is a battlefield where groups fight over its meaning. ⚠ controversial = provokes strong reaction; contested = rival definitions or claims in play.
ex: "Harm" remains a contested concept in debates over regulating hate speech.

words.en: to publicly and strongly declare that someone or something is wrong or evil
words.usage: denounce X as Y (denounce the policy as racist); publicly / strongly denounce; denounce someone to the authorities (= report, inform on); denunciation (n.)
words.ety: Latin de- (down, against) + nuntiare (to announce); cf. announce, pronounce, renounce
words.tip: de-nounce = announce against: loud, public condemnation, not quiet criticism. ⚠ denounce (publicly condemn) vs. renounce (give up, reject for oneself).
words.text: "President George W. Bush denounced outrageous conspiracy theories about 9/11 while his own administration was busy promoting the outrageous conspiracy theory that Iraq was behind 9/11"
ex: The UN denounced the attack on civilians.
She was denounced by her own party for the remarks.
Students gathered to denounce the tuition hike.
The church denounced the film as immoral.
Many scholars have denounced hate speech as a form of violence, while others warn against equating words with physical harm.

words.en: n. a strong verbal or written attack on someone's views; adj. aggressively argumentative, written to attack rather than to weigh both sides
words.ko: n. 논박, 논쟁적 글 / adj. 논쟁적인, 공격적인
words.usage: a polemic against + view / person; a polemical essay / tone / style; polemically charged; engage in polemics
words.ety: Greek polemos (war); polemikos (warlike); cf. polemicist
words.tip: polemos = war, so a polemic is war fought with words. ⚠ polemical (attacks one side) ≠ contested (has rival sides) ≠ controversial (provokes strong reaction).
ex: Read as a polemic against free speech absolutism, the book overstates the case for banning slurs.

words.en: the quality of being clear, logical, and convincing
words.ko: (논증의) 설득력, 타당성; cogent = 설득력 있는, 논리가 탄탄한
words.usage: a cogent argument / case / critique / explanation; the cogency of + argument/claim; question / doubt the cogency of X; lack cogency; (logic) cogent (inductive) vs. sound (deductive)
words.ety: Latin cogere (to drive together, compel): co- (together) + agere (to drive); cf. cogent, agent, act
words.tip: co + agere = drive together → an argument that herds your thinking into agreement. ⚠ Stronger than plausible (그럴듯한): cogent = hard to resist.
ex: She gave a cogent explanation of why we should take the train instead of driving.
His excuse lacked cogency; nobody believed him.
The report makes a cogent case for raising the minimum wage.
Students learn to judge the cogency of an argument, not just whether they agree with it.
Critics doubt the cogency of the claim that counter-speech is always enough to answer hate speech.

words.en: impossible to attack, challenge, or defeat
words.ko: 공격(반박)할 수 없는, 확고한, 난공불락의; assail = 공격하다, (비판을) 퍼붓다
words.usage: an unassailable argument / position / lead / truth; treat X as unassailable; seemingly unassailable; assail X with criticism
words.ety: un- + assail + -able; assail from Latin ad- (toward) + salire (to leap); cf. assault, salient, sally
words.tip: assail = leap at to attack → unassailable = a wall nobody can leap at and take. Same salire (to leap) as salient (already in your bank). ⚠ Stronger than cogent: cogent = hard to refute; unassailable = cannot be refuted. In critique, 'treated as unassailable' = the author is about to challenge it.
ex: With a 20-point lead at halftime, the team looked unassailable.
Her alibi was unassailable: three people saw her at the café.
The company's position in the market once seemed unassailable.
Teachers should not present textbook claims as unassailable truths.
Free speech absolutists often treat the "marketplace of ideas" as unassailable, but critics ask who is shut out of that market.

words.en: (n.) an act that treats someone as unimportant; a snub or insult. (v.) to treat someone with disregard
words.usage: a slight (to/on/against someone); take something as a slight; feel slighted; slight someone (by doing); a perceived slight; no slight intended
words.ety: From the adjective slight 'small, thin, unimportant' (Old English/Old Norse sléttr 'smooth, plain'). To slight someone = to treat them as slight (unimportant). Related: slightly, slighting
words.tip: Same word as 'slight = small': a slight treats you as small, as if you don't matter. ⚠ noun 'a slight' (모욕) vs. adjective 'slight' (약간의)
words.text: "Anger is caused by a slight and it motivates revenge."
ex: She felt slighted when her friends made dinner plans without her.
Forgetting his name at the party was an accidental slight, not an insult.
He took the late reply as a personal slight.
No slight intended, but I think the first draft was clearer.
For Aristotle, anger is a response to a perceived slight, a sense that one has been treated as worthless by someone who should not have done so.

words.en: to give or ascribe value to something; to treat it as admirable (often uncritically)
words.ko: 가치를 부여하다, 높이 평가하다, (때로) 치켜세우다·미화하다; valorization = 가치 부여, (마르크스) 가치 증식 (↔ devalue, denigrate)
words.usage: valorize + value / practice / group; valorize X over Y; tend to valorize + noun; the valorization of + noun
words.ety: Latin valor (worth, value), from valere (to be strong, be worth) + -ize; cf. value, evaluate, valid, valiant, devalue
words.tip: valor + -ize = put a value on it (value + -ize). In critical writing, 'X valorizes Y' often hints: Y is praised as good, but should it be?
ex: Our family has always valorized hard work over talent.
Some films valorize violence by making the killer look heroic.
Modern culture tends to valorize being busy, as if rest were a weakness.
A bilingual curriculum can valorize students' home languages instead of treating them as obstacles.
When a community valorizes "saying what you think," slurs can be defended as mere honesty.

words.en: to formally deny that you have responsibility for, knowledge of, or a connection to something
words.ko: (책임·관련을) 부인하다, 거부하다; disclaimer = 면책 조항, 부인 성명
words.usage: disclaim + responsibility / knowledge / any intention to + verb / authorship; disclaim that + clause; issue / add a disclaimer
words.ety: Anglo-French des- 'away, apart' + clamer 'to claim' (Latin clamare 'to call out'); cf. claim, exclaim, proclaim, clamor
words.tip: dis-claim = un-claim: you push a claim away from yourself. ⚠ disclaim (deny it's mine) vs. deny (say it isn't true) vs. renounce (give up something I had).
ex: The company disclaimed any responsibility for the damage.
The video starts with a disclaimer that it isn't medical advice.
She disclaimed any knowledge of the missing files.
The author disclaims any intention to settle the debate; she only wants to clarify its terms.
A speaker who disclaims hateful intent does not thereby undo the injury his words have done.

words.en: claimed to be true but not proven
words.usage: the alleged + noun (the alleged neutrality); X is alleged to be Y
words.ety: From allege (to claim), via Old French
words.tip: Courtroom: the "alleged" thief is claimed guilty, not yet proven.
words.text: "acknowledgement of the alleged pupil's judgment" (p. 54); "the alleged predicament" (p. 57) / "the alleged protocols were used to justify the massacres of Jews" (p. 14); "for the study of this or that alleged conspiracy" (p. 25)
words.source: Noddings Ch. 3, pp. 54, 57 / Cassam, Conspiracy Theories, Ch. 1, pp. 14, 25
ex: The alleged thief was released because of a lack of evidence.
She denied the alleged affair in a press interview.
The newspaper reported the alleged abuse to the police.
The alleged neutrality of the method hides its value commitments.
Holocaust deniers cite alleged "gaps" in the evidence while ignoring the vast documentary record.

words.en: not seeming reasonable or likely to be true (opp. plausible = seeming reasonable)
words.ko: 믿기 어려운, 개연성이 낮은 (반. plausible = 그럴듯한)
words.usage: highly / wildly implausible; implausible by design; it is implausible that + clause; an implausible claim / explanation / excuse; implausibility (n.); syn. far-fetched, improbable
words.ety: im- (not) + Latin plaudere (to clap, applaud); cf. applause, applaud, explode (orig. 'clap off the stage')
words.tip: plausible = worth applause = believable; im-plausible = no applause = hard to believe. ⚠ Don't flip it: plausible = 그럴듯한, implausible = 그럴듯하지 않은.
words.text: "given the features ... they're unlikely to be true. ... Conspiracy Theories are implausible by design."
ex: His excuse that the dog ate his homework sounded implausible.
It's implausible that she finished the whole book in one hour.
The movie's plot was so implausible that nobody in the theater believed it.
Investigators found the suspect's alibi highly implausible.
It is implausible to claim that a single slur causes no harm simply because no physical injury occurs.

words.en: to search persistently for something hidden and find it
words.usage: ferret out + hidden thing (assumptions, values, bias)
words.ety: A ferret is a small animal once used to chase rabbits out of their burrows
words.tip: Picture a ferret digging a hidden value out of its burrow.
words.text: "a better approach ... is to ferret out these values, confess them, and build one's case frankly on them"
ex: The study ferrets out the hidden curriculum in textbook images.

words.en: (adj.) clear and obvious to see; (v.) to show itself clearly, so that something inner or abstract (a feeling, quality, symptom, belief) becomes visible in behavior or events / manifestation (n.): a visible sign or form of something underlying
words.ko: (adj.) 명백한, 분명한; (v.) (감정·증상·성질 등이) 겉으로 드러나다, 나타나다 / manifestation = (숨은 것이) 드러난 모습, 발현, 표출, 징후 (≠ 단순한 '현상' phenomenon)
words.usage: X manifests itself in / as Y; X manifests in Y; manifest symptoms / signs of X; a manifest failure / error / injustice; manifestly unfair / absurd / false / a manifestation of X; one / another manifestation of X
words.ety: Latin manifestus ('palpable, caught in the act'), from manus (hand) + -festus (struck); cf. manual, manuscript
words.tip: manus = hand: so plain you could catch or touch it with your hand. Unlike 'show' or 'demonstrate', 'manifest' suggests that something inside surfaces on its own, not that someone deliberately displays it. / manifestation = the tip of the iceberg: the visible part of a hidden X, so always ask 'a manifestation of what?'
ex: His nervousness manifested itself in a tapping foot all through the meeting.
The illness can manifest as fatigue long before other symptoms appear.
It was a manifest injustice that the students were never given a chance to respond.
Her interest in philosophy first manifested in childhood, when she kept asking 'why?' about everything.

Prejudice rarely announces itself; it manifests in everyday word choices, tone, and who gets interrupted.

manifestation:
A fever is a manifestation of the body fighting an infection.
Her constant joking was a manifestation of her nervousness.
Graffiti on the mosque was seen as one manifestation of rising hostility toward Muslims.
Bullying is often a manifestation of deeper problems in a school's culture.
On this view, a single slur is not an isolated insult but a manifestation of a larger system of subordination.

words.en: thoroughly filled or permeated with something
words.usage: X is shot through with + noun (values, assumptions, tension)
words.ety: Weaving: to "shoot" a thread of another color across the cloth
words.tip: Picture colored threads woven through the whole fabric. Values are woven into analysis.
words.text: "analytic work and theory itself are both shot through with values"
ex: Her account of school discipline is shot through with assumptions about race.

words.en: the process or state of coming together toward the same point, view, or conclusion
words.usage: a convergence of / between X and Y; points of convergence; converge on / upon + conclusion; converge with + view
words.ety: Latin con- (together) + vergere (to bend, turn toward); cf. diverge, verge
words.tip: Picture lines bending toward one point. ⚠ Opposite: divergence (lines spreading apart).
ex: There is a striking convergence between Butler's and Langton's accounts of how speech can subordinate.

words.en: adj. done on purpose; v. to think about or discuss carefully before deciding
words.ko: adj. 의도적인, 신중한 / v. 숙의하다, 숙고하다
words.usage: adj. a deliberate act / choice; deliberately exclude; v. deliberate about / on / over + issue; deliberative democracy; democratic deliberation
words.ety: Latin de- (thoroughly) + librare (to weigh), from libra (scales); cf. Libra, equilibrium
words.tip: Libra = scales. To deliberate is to weigh reasons on a scale, together. ⚠ Pronunciation: adj. -rət, verb -rayt.
ex: Students deliberated over whether the school should ban the offensive mascot.

words.en: to adopt or publicly support a belief, value, or cause
words.ko: (신념·주의를) 지지하다, 신봉하다, 표방하다; espoused values = (결으로) 표방하는 가치
words.usage: espouse a view / belief / cause / values; espoused theory vs. theory-in-use (Argyris & Schön); espoused vs. enacted values; an espoused commitment to + noun
words.ety: Latin sponsare (to betroth), from spondere (to promise solemnly); cf. spouse, sponsor, respond, responsible
words.tip: Spouse is hidden inside: to espouse a belief = to marry it. ⚠ 'espoused' often hints at a gap between what is professed and what is actually done (espoused vs. enacted).
ex: My grandmother espoused a simple rule: never waste food.
He espouses healthy eating but lives on instant noodles.
The party espouses lower taxes and smaller government.
Many schools espouse inclusion, yet their discipline data tell a different story.
A school's espoused commitment to respect means little if teachers let slurs go unchallenged.

words.en: to put forward a claim or assumption as a starting point for argument, without proving it first
words.usage: posit that + clause; posit X as Y; posit the existence of X; a posited entity / a posited cause; positing (n./gerund): 'in positing X, the author assumes ...'
words.ety: Latin ponere / positus (to put, place); cf. position, position, compose, propose, suppose
words.tip: To posit = to put a claim down on the table as a starting point. Like 'position' (where something is put) and 'suppose' (put under). Stronger than 'suggest', weaker than 'prove'; the claim is assumed, not yet demonstrated.
ex: Detectives often posit a motive before they have any evidence, so they can test it.
Let's posit that everyone arrives by 9 a.m.; how should we plan the day?
Early astronomers posited the existence of an unseen planet to explain Uranus's odd orbit.
In positing a single 'true' meaning of the text, the author overlooks other readings.
Austin posits that saying certain words can itself perform an action.

words.en: a person who argues for or supports an idea, theory, or plan
words.usage: a proponent of + idea / view / theory (a proponent of free speech); a leading / strong / vocal proponent; proponents and opponents; opp. opponent, critic
words.ety: Latin pro- (forward) + ponere (to put, place): 'one who puts forward'; cf. propose, proposition, posit, opponent, component
words.tip: pro-pon-ent = puts an idea forward (like propose); op-pon-ent = puts against. ⚠ proponent (지지자) vs. opponent (반대자); 'an insincere proponent' = someone who pushes a view without believing it.
words.text: "... than an insincere proponent of the same view"
ex: She is a strong proponent of eating breakfast every day.
Proponents of the new subway line say it will cut traffic.
He became a vocal proponent of remote work during the pandemic.
Proponents and opponents of the bill debated for hours.
Proponents of strong free speech protections often worry that banning hate speech will silence minority voices too.

words.en: the reasons or logic behind a decision, belief, or action
words.usage: the rationale behind / for X; provide / offer / explain a rationale; a clear / strong / underlying rationale; the rationale of this study (academic)
words.ety: Latin ratio (reason, calculation) → rationalis; cf. rational, reason, ratio, rationalize
words.tip: rationale = the bundle of reasons behind a choice, the tidy answer to 'Why did you do that?' ⚠ rationale (n., rash-uh-NAL) vs. rational (adj., 합리적인).
words.source: Asked while reading Cassam, Conspiracy Theories, Ch. 1
ex: Can you explain the rationale behind the new parking rules?
The teacher shared her rationale for grouping students by interest.
The company never gave a clear rationale for the layoffs.
Each grant proposal must include a rationale explaining why the project matters.
Cassam's rationale for calling Conspiracy Theories propaganda is that their features make them unlikely to be true, so their real function must lie elsewhere.

words.en: 1) to move troops, people, or resources into position for action; 2) (academic) to bring a concept, argument, or strategy into use for a specific purpose
words.ko: 1) (군대·인력·자원을) 배치하다, 투입하다; 2) (개념·논증·전략을 목적에 맞게) 활용하다, 동원하다
words.usage: deploy troops / resources / staff; deploy + concept / argument / strategy / term + to do X; deploy X against Y; be deployed in / as; deployment (n.)
words.ety: Old French desployer (to unfold), Latin dis- (apart) + plicare (to fold); cf. display, explicate, imply
words.tip: de-ploy = unfold: an army unfolding into position, or an author unfolding a concept and putting it to work. ⚠ Not the same as apply (적용하다). deploy suggests strategic, purposeful use; apply = put a rule or theory onto a case.
ex: The city deployed extra police officers for the marathon.
The company plans to deploy the new software next month.
Rescue teams were deployed within hours of the earthquake.
Butler deploys Austin's notion of the performative to show how speech can injure.
The term 'free speech' is often deployed to shut down criticism rather than to protect it.

words.en: acceptable or agreeable to someone (literally: pleasant to taste)
words.ko: 받아들일 만한, 입맛에 맞는 / 받아들이기 힘든
words.usage: palatable to + someone (palatable to conspiracy theorists); make X more palatable; an unpalatable truth / conclusion
words.ety: palate (roof of the mouth, sense of taste) + -able; cf. palate, palatial (⚠ unrelated: from Palatine Hill)
words.tip: Pleasing to the palate = easy to swallow. An idea that is palatable goes down easily; an unpalatable truth is hard to swallow.
words.text: "I don't suppose that what I say in this book will be any more palatable to conspiracy theorists and their apologists."
words.source: Cassam, Conspiracy Theories, Preface, p. vii
ex: The soup was barely palatable, but we were too hungry to care.
She tried to make the bad news more palatable by starting with a joke.
A four-day work week is a palatable idea to most employees.
The compromise was palatable to both parties, so the bill passed.
Cassam doubts that his political reading of conspiracy theories will be any more palatable to their defenders than his earlier article was.

words.en: 1) to invent a story, excuse, or plan (often to deceive); 2) to make a dish or drink by mixing ingredients
words.usage: concoct + story / excuse / plan / scheme / myth; concoct X out of / from Y; a myth concocted to serve X; a strange concoction (n.); syn. fabricate, make up, cook up
words.ety: Latin con- (together) + coquere (to cook): 'cook together'; cf. cook, cuisine, precocious, biscuit
words.tip: Cook it up: stir bits of fact and fantasy in one pot until a believable story comes out. Implies deliberate invention, not honest error. ⚠ concoct = mixed together with some effort; fabricate = flatly fake.
words.text: "The theory that the Holocaust is a myth concocted to serve Jewish interests is."
ex: She concocted a delicious drink out of mango, lime, and mint.
He concocted an excuse about a flat tire to explain why he was late.
The children concocted a plan to surprise their teacher on her birthday.
The tabloid concocted a scandal out of a single blurry photo.
Some hate groups concoct histories of victimhood to justify hostility toward minorities.

words.en: a trick or false story meant to make people believe something that is not true
words.usage: an elaborate hoax; a hoax call / bomb hoax; turn out to be a hoax; claim that X was a hoax; hoax (v.) someone; hoaxer (n.)
words.ety: Probably a shortening of hocus (as in hocus-pocus, a magician's trick words), late 18th c.
words.tip: Hocus-pocus: a magician's trick on a large scale. A hoax is deliberately staged to fool people, not an honest mistake.
words.text: "Conspiracy Theorists started to claim that the whole episode was an elaborate hoax by the government"
ex: The 'free phone' message turned out to be a hoax.
Police received a bomb hoax and evacuated the station.
The famous photo of the monster was later revealed as a hoax.
Some people still claim the moon landing was a hoax.
Calling a massacre a 'hoax' does more than spread a falsehood; it insults the victims and their grieving families.

words.en: to bring about or cause; to lead someone to do something
words.usage: induce + noun (learning, shame); induce someone to do something
words.ety: Latin in- (into) + ducere (to lead); cf. produce, introduce, educate
words.tip: Induce leads learning in; educate (e-ducere) leads it out.
words.text: "Dewey insisted that teaching should induce learning"
ex: Repeated exposure to slurs can induce a lasting sense of shame.

words.en: to prevent something, or make it impossible in advance
words.usage: preclude + noun; preclude someone from doing something
words.ety: Latin prae- (before) + claudere (to shut); cf. include, exclude, conclude, seclude
words.tip: Shutting the door beforehand. Opposites: allow, permit, make possible.
words.text: "whether, e.g., the pupil is not systematically precluded from asking 'How?' 'Why?'"
ex: Calling analysis neutral can preclude honest discussion of its values.

words.en: to persuade someone NOT to do something; to talk someone out of a plan or action
words.usage: dissuade someone from doing / from + noun; try / attempt to dissuade; be dissuaded by + reason; dissuasion (n.); dissuasive (adj.)
words.ety: Latin dis- (apart, away) + suadere (to urge, advise); cf. persuade, suave, suasion
words.tip: per-suade = urge someone TOWARD it; dis-suade = urge someone AWAY from it. Same root, opposite direction. ⚠ Always 'dissuade from doing', never 'dissuade to do'. vs. deter: deter works through fear of consequences; dissuade works through advice or argument.
ex: My friends tried to dissuade me from quitting my job, but I had already decided.
Nothing could dissuade her from moving abroad for her PhD.
The heavy rain didn't dissuade the fans from lining up outside the stadium.
High tuition costs may dissuade first-generation students from applying to graduate school.
Some argue that school speech codes dissuade students from voicing unpopular views, not just hateful ones.

words.en: a strong, earnest urging to do something (often moral or sermon-like)
words.ko: 간곡한 권고, 열렬한 촉구, 훈계; exhort = 간곡히 권하다, 촉구하다
words.usage: exhort someone to do something; an exhortation to + noun / to do; mere / moral exhortation; despite someone's exhortations
words.ety: Latin ex- (thoroughly) + hortari (to urge, encourage); cf. hortatory
words.tip: ex + hortari = push hard from behind → an urgent, preachy 'You must do this!' ⚠ exhort (push toward doing) vs. dissuade (hold back from doing). In critique, 'mere exhortation' = only telling people to be good, with no real mechanism for change.
ex: Despite his mother's exhortations, he still didn't clean his room.
The coach's halftime exhortation fired up the whole team.
The president's speech was full of exhortations to unity.
Exhortations to "be kind" do little unless schools also change how they handle conflict.
Critics argue that answering hate speech with moral exhortation alone leaves its structural harms untouched.

words.en: gradually damaging or destroying something (originally: eating away metal)
words.usage: corrosive to + noun (corrosive to well-being / trust / democracy); have a corrosive effect on X; corrode + trust / institutions; the corrosion of X
words.ety: Latin cor- (thoroughly) + rodere (to gnaw); cf. rodent, erode, erosion
words.tip: rodere = gnaw, like a rodent. Corrosive damage is slow and hidden, like rust eating through metal. ⚠ corrode (gnawed through, often chemical or moral) vs. erode (worn away from outside, gradually).
words.text: "A recent study describes their theories as corrosive to societal and individual well-being."
ex: Salt water is highly corrosive to metal car parts.
Constant criticism can be corrosive to a child's self-confidence.
Lying, even about small things, has a corrosive effect on a friendship.
Some scholars argue that misinformation is corrosive to democratic trust.
Hate speech is corrosive not only to its targets but to the shared norms of a classroom community.

words.en: to make something (usually bad) continue indefinitely
words.ko: (나쁜 것을) 영속시키다, 계속 이어지게 하다, 존속시키다; perpetuation = 영속화, 지속
words.usage: perpetuate + stereotypes / inequality / injustice / a myth / a cycle of violence; serve to perpetuate; (unwittingly) perpetuate X; the perpetuation of + noun
words.ety: Latin perpetuus (continuous, uninterrupted), from per- (through) + petere (to go toward, seek); cf. perpetual, perpetuity
words.tip: perpetual = endless → perpetuate = keep it going without a break. ⚠ perpetuate (지속시키다) vs. perpetrate (저지르다; perpetrator = 가해자): perpet-U-ate = contin-U-e; perpe-TR-ate = commit TRouble.
ex: Telling kids "boys don't cry" perpetuates old ideas about masculinity.
Skipping the doctor because you're afraid only perpetuates the worry.
Housing policies can perpetuate racial segregation for generations.
Tracking students by ability early may perpetuate the very gaps it claims to address.
Even "harmless" jokes can perpetuate the stereotypes that give slurs their power to wound.

words.en: 1) (v.) to crush into small bits or powder; 2) (n.) hard, dull, repetitive work; 3) (v.) to keep working or studying hard at something tedious
words.ko: 1) 갈다, 빻다; 2) 고되고 지루한 일, 반복 노동; 3) 꾸준히 힘들게 하다, 열심히 공부하다
words.usage: grind + coffee / grain; the daily grind; a long grind; grind away at + task; grind through + work; grind out + result (힘들게 뽑아내다); grind to a halt (서서히 멈추다)
words.ety: Old English grindan (to crush, rub); cf. grindstone, keep your nose to the grindstone (= work hard nonstop)
words.tip: Picture a millstone going round and round: the same slow, heavy motion, over and over. Grinding work wears you down the way stone wears down grain.
ex: I grind fresh coffee beans every morning.
After the holidays, it's back to the daily grind.
She spent the weekend grinding away at her dissertation proposal.
Traffic ground to a halt on the highway.
Doctoral study is less a series of breakthroughs than a long grind of reading, writing, and revising.

words.en: finding it very difficult to do something
words.usage: be hard pressed to do something; would be hard pressed to find / explain
words.ety: press (squeeze) + hard (strongly)
words.tip: Someone pressed hard against a wall with no room to move.
words.text: "Many of us ... would be hard pressed if asked to spell out in simple words the ideas"
ex: You would be hard pressed to find a teacher who has never felt burned out.

words.en: to free someone or something from a tangle, trap, or difficult situation, usually with effort
words.usage: extricate oneself / someone from + situation / place; extricate X from Y; find it hard to extricate oneself; extrication (n.); inextricable / inextricably linked (adj./adv.)
words.ety: Latin ex- (out) + tricae (tangles, perplexities); cf. intricate (tangled in), inextricable
words.tip: ex + tricae = out of the tangle; intricate = in the tangle. ⚠ inextricably linked = so tangled together they can't be separated (very common in academic writing). Implies effort: you struggle out, you don't just leave.
ex: It took the firefighters an hour to extricate the driver from the wrecked car.
The cat got tangled in the yarn and couldn't extricate itself.
He told a small lie and then couldn't extricate himself from it.
Once a country enters a war, extricating itself can take decades.
Butler suggests that the subject can never fully extricate itself from the language that wounds it; injury and identity are inextricably linked.

words.en: a difficult situation that is hard to get out of
words.usage: be in a predicament; face a predicament; an intellectual / moral predicament
words.ety: Late Latin praedicamentum (something asserted); cf. predicate
words.tip: Usually "in a predicament" or "face a predicament." Intellectual predicament = 지적 곤경.
words.text: "given their intellectual predicaments"
ex: Many first-year PhD students face the same predicament: too much reading, too little time.

words.en: able to exist or be true together without contradiction
words.usage: X is compatible with Y; perfectly / logically compatible with; incompatible with; compatibility (n.)
words.ety: Latin com- (together) + pati (to suffer, endure): 'able to endure together'; cf. patient, passion, sympathy
words.tip: Like a charger compatible with your phone: they fit and work together. In philosophy: two claims can both be true at once.
words.text: "So 'speculative' as I understand it is compatible with 'already disproved'."
ex: This charger isn't compatible with my new phone.
Is the software compatible with Windows?
Their schedules weren't compatible, so they rarely met.
Free will may be compatible with determinism, some philosophers argue.
Protecting free speech is compatible with restricting targeted harassment.

words.en: (of a word) to suggest an associated feeling or idea beyond its literal meaning
words.ko: 함축하다, (부가적 의미·어감을) 내포하다; connotation = 함축, 어감 (↔ denote 직접 가리키다)
words.usage: X connotes Y; connote + feeling / quality / idea; positive / negative connotation; carry (a) connotation(s) of; denote vs. connote
words.ety: Latin con- (together, with) + notare (to mark), from nota (a mark); cf. note, notation, denote, notable
words.tip: con- = with, note = mark → a mark that comes along WITH the word. ⚠ denote = what the word directly points to (dictionary meaning); connote = the feeling that tags along (connotation). Think: denote = directly, connote = context.
ex: "Home" connotes warmth and safety, not just a building.
For many people, the word "cheap" connotes poor quality.
The label "illegal" connotes criminality in a way that "undocumented" does not.
Even when a slur denotes a group neutrally, it connotes contempt toward its members.
In educational discourse, "achievement gap" can connote a deficit in students rather than in the system.

words.en: (of a word or sign) to directly refer to or stand for something; to indicate
words.ko: 나타내다, 가리키다, 의미하다; denotation = 외연, 사전적 의미 (↔ connotation 함축, 내포)
words.usage: X denotes Y; the term denotes + noun; be denoted by + symbol; used to denote + noun
words.ety: Latin de- (down, completely) + notare (to mark), from nota (a mark, sign); cf. note, notation, connote
words.tip: de + note = 딱 표시해 두다 → 직접 가리키는 뜻. ⚠ denote vs. connote: denote = 사전에 적힌 뜻, connote (con = with) = 같이 따라오는 느낌·함축
ex: A red light denotes that you must stop.
On this map, a small star denotes a capital city.
In the chart, the dotted line denotes the national average.
The word 'home' denotes a place where one lives, but it connotes warmth and belonging.
A slur may denote a group neutrally on paper, yet what it does in use goes far beyond what it denotes.

words.en: a method of reasoning that advances through the tension between opposing ideas (Socratic questioning; Hegel's movement through contradiction; Marx's dialectical materialism)
words.ko: 변증법, (대립을 통한) 논증·사유의 방법; dialectical = 변증법적인, (긴장 속에서) 서로를 만들어 가는
words.usage: Socratic / Hegelian / Marxist dialectic; a dialectic between X and Y; a dialectical relationship / process / tension; dialectical materialism; thesis–antithesis–synthesis (simplified Hegel)
words.ety: Greek dialektikē (art of conversation), from dia- (across, through) + legein (to speak); cf. dialogue, dialect
words.tip: dia + legein = talking back and forth → ideas move forward by answering each other. Same root as dialogue. 'A dialectical relationship' = two things shaping each other through tension, not one simply determining the other. ⚠ thesis–antithesis–synthesis is a textbook simplification of Hegel.
ex: Our long argument turned into a kind of dialectic: each objection pushed us to a better plan.
Socratic dialectic exposes contradictions in what people think they know.
Marx borrowed Hegel's dialectic but grounded it in economic conditions.
Freire describes a dialectical relationship in which teachers and students learn from each other.
Butler sees a dialectic between injury and agency: the name that wounds can also become a site of resistance.

words.en: relating to questions and the logic of asking and answering
words.usage: an erotetic concept / approach / logic
words.ety: Greek erōtan (to ask)
words.tip: Think of Socrates, who taught in Greek by asking questions. ⚠ Unrelated to "erotic."
words.text: "Macmillan and Garrison have introduced an 'erotetic' concept of teaching."
ex: An erotetic approach plans lessons around the questions students ought to ask.

words.en: (of words or language) used in a non-literal way, through metaphor or other figures of speech, to suggest a meaning beyond the words themselves
words.ko: 비유적인, 비유적 의미의 (↔ 문자 그대로의 literal)
words.usage: figurative language / meaning / sense / expression; in a figurative sense; used figuratively; figuratively speaking; figurative vs. literal
words.ety: Latin figura (shape, form; figure of speech), from fingere (to shape, form); cf. figure, fiction, feign
words.tip: figura = a shape. Figurative language reshapes words so they mean more than they say. A 'figure of speech' is exactly that: words bent into a new shape. ⚠ Opposite: literal. People often misuse 'literally' when they mean 'figuratively' ('I literally died laughing').
ex: When she said her boss 'exploded,' she was speaking figuratively.
'Break the ice' is a figurative expression; no actual ice is involved.
Children often take figurative language literally and get confused.
Poetry relies heavily on figurative language such as metaphor and simile.
Butler argues that the language of 'wounding' words is not merely figurative: speech can injure in a real sense.

words.en: relating to sentence structure and word order
words.usage: syntactic analysis / structure; syntactically correct
words.ety: Greek syn- (together) + taxis (arrangement)
words.tip: Syntax = how words are arranged together. Compare semantic = meaning.
words.text: "Syntactic analysis is an important part of this approach."
ex: The sentence is syntactically correct but semantically empty.

words.en: a book or tool that lists words grouped by similar meaning (synonyms), and sometimes opposites, to help you find the right word
words.ko: 유의어 사전, 동의어 사전 (뜯이 비슷한 단어를 묶어 둔 사전)
words.usage: look it up in a thesaurus; use a thesaurus to find a synonym for X; an online thesaurus; plural: thesauri / thesauruses; thesaurus vs. dictionary
words.ety: Greek thesauros (treasure, storehouse), via Latin thesaurus; cf. treasure
words.tip: Same root as 'treasure': a thesaurus is a treasure house of words. ⚠ Dictionary = what a word means; thesaurus = which other words mean something similar. Tip: check nuance in a dictionary before swapping a word, since synonyms are rarely identical.
words.text: "The Well-Spoken Thesaurus" (book title)
ex: I couldn't think of another word for 'happy,' so I checked a thesaurus.
Writers keep a thesaurus nearby to avoid repeating the same word.
A thesaurus lists 'big,' 'huge,' and 'enormous' together, but each has a different feel.
Don't swap words blindly from a thesaurus; 'thin' and 'skinny' are not interchangeable in formal writing.
Her essay read as awkward because she had substituted rare thesaurus words for precise ones, so 'harm' became 'detriment' where it didn't fit.

words.en: a fact or condition that happens to hold but could have been otherwise, and for no deeper reason or justification (a matter of mere chance, not of principle or desert) / contingency: (philosophy) the state of being possible but not necessary; (everyday) a possible future event, an emergency
words.ko: 자의적 우연(성), 아무 근거 없이 그저 그렇게 된 우연한 사실 / contingency = 우연성, 우발성 (↔ necessity 필연성); 만일의 사태, 비상사태; contingent on = ~에 달린 (⚠ 일관성은 consistency)
words.usage: the arbitrary contingency of birth / history / X; X is (merely) an arbitrary contingency; treat X as an arbitrary contingency rather than a necessity; contingent on / upon Y (= depends on Y); morally arbitrary (Rawls); the contingency of + norms / meaning; a contingency plan; as a contingency
words.ety: arbitrary: Latin arbiter (judge), i.e. left to someone's whim, not a rule; contingency: Latin con- (together) + tangere (to touch): things that 'touch' / happen together by chance; cf. tangent, contact, arbitration
words.tip: arbitrary = no reason; contingent = could have been otherwise (opposite: necessary). Put together: it just happened to be so, and nothing justifies it. ⚠ Common critical move: showing that something presented as natural or necessary is really an arbitrary contingency. ⚠ contingency (tang = touch → chance) vs. consistency (sist = stand → standing steady, 일관성).
ex: Where you are born is an arbitrary contingency, yet it shapes almost everything about your life.
The rule that the oldest child inherits the house is an arbitrary contingency of local custom, not a law of nature.
Rawls calls natural talents 'morally arbitrary': no one deserves the contingencies of the natural lottery.
Which words count as slurs is not an arbitrary contingency; it tracks histories of violence and exclusion.

By showing that gender norms are historical, Butler exposes as arbitrary contingency what had seemed a natural necessity.

contingency / contingent:
We packed extra water as a contingency in case the hike took longer.
The school has a contingency plan for snow days.
Our trip is contingent on the weather.
Historians stress the contingency of events: things could easily have turned out differently.
Showing the contingency of a slur's meaning opens the possibility that it can be resisted or resignified.

words.en: (adj.) convenient and useful for a purpose, though possibly not right or fair; (n.) a quick means to an end
words.ko: (당장) 편리한, 편의주의적인, 방편적인; (n.) 방편, 임시방편; expediency = 편의주의
words.usage: it is expedient (for someone) to + verb; politically / administratively expedient; a temporary / simple expedient; out of expediency; expediency over principle
words.ety: Latin expedire 'to free the feet': ex- 'out' + pes, ped- 'foot' (freeing feet from a trap → making things go easily); cf. expedite, expedition, impede, pedal
words.tip: ex + ped = feet out of the trap → things move fast and easily. But the 'easy way' often isn't the right way. ⚠ expedient (convenient, often morally suspect) vs. efficient (works well, neutral) vs. expeditious (done quickly).
ex: It was expedient to take a taxi since the bus was late.
Taping the broken window was only a temporary expedient.
The politician changed his position because it was politically expedient.
Banning the book was an expedient response that avoided any real conversation about racism.
Treating hate speech as a mere discipline issue may be administratively expedient, but it ignores the harm to the students targeted.

words.en: a standard or test used to judge something (plural: criteria)
words.usage: meet / satisfy a criterion; the criteria for X
words.ety: Greek kritēs (judge); cf. critic, critical
words.tip: ⚠ One criterion, two criteria (like phenomenon / phenomena). Never "a criteria."
words.text: "Scheffler argued that teaching is characterized by three criteria"
ex: The intentionality criterion is the least controversial of the three.

words.en: a range in which things change gradually from one end to the other
words.usage: on a continuum; at one end of the continuum; a continuum from X to Y
words.ety: Latin continuus (uninterrupted); cf. continue
words.tip: Something that continues without breaks.
words.text: "With this continuum in place, Green invites us to consider a 'region of intelligence.'"
ex: Instruction and indoctrination may sit on a continuum rather than in separate boxes.

words.en: one particular aspect or side of something complex; originally, one of the small flat surfaces of a cut gem
words.usage: a facet of X; one / another / every facet of X; a key / overlooked / different facet; facets of identity; multifaceted / many-faceted (adj.)
words.ety: French facette, a diminutive of face (from Latin facies, 'face'); i.e. 'little face'
words.tip: A cut gem has many small flat faces, and each catches the light differently. In the same way, a complex issue has many facets, each showing one side of it. A 'facet' is a part you look at one at a time, so it's less than the 'whole', and it works well with multifaceted.
ex: Cooking is just one facet of her many talents.
The diamond's facets caught the light and scattered it across the wall.
Moving abroad changed every facet of his daily life.
Hate speech has a legal facet, a moral facet, and an educational facet.
This paper examines only one facet of the problem: how teachers respond in the moment.

words.en: (n.) nearness in space, time, or relationship
words.usage: in (close) proximity to X; the proximity of A to B; proximity between A and B; proximate cause (직접 원인) vs. distal/ultimate cause
words.ety: Latin proximus 'nearest' (from prope 'near'). Related: approximate (거의 가까운, 근사치), proximal
words.tip: approximate = almost (nearly) right → proximity = nearness. Formal version of 'closeness'
ex: We chose the apartment for its proximity to campus.
The two cats sleep in close proximity on cold nights.
Living in close proximity to a highway can affect children's health.
Schools in close proximity to each other often compete for the same students.
Freud's account brings love and hate into uncomfortable proximity, suggesting they are closer than we usually admit.

words.en: a map of how things are positioned in relation to each other
words.usage: construct / offer a topology of X
words.ety: Greek topos (place) + -logy (study)
words.tip: topos = place, so a map of places. ⚠ Not typology (sorting into types).
words.text: "Thomas Green constructed a topology of the teaching concept."
ex: She offers a topology of harmful speech, from insults to threats.

words.en: the process of gaining a skill, knowledge, or habit (e.g. language acquisition); also, something bought or obtained, or one company buying another
words.usage: acquisition of + skill/knowledge/language; (second) language acquisition (제2언어 습득); vocabulary acquisition; acquire a habit/taste/skill; acquired taste (점차 좋아하게 되는 것); a recent acquisition
words.ety: Latin ad- 'to' + quaerere 'to seek' → 'seek and get.' Same root: inquire, question, request, conquest, exquisite
words.tip: quaer/quis = seek (question, inquire, request) → ac-QUIS-ition = what you sought and finally got. In SLA, 'acquisition' (natural, unconscious) is often contrasted with 'learning' (conscious study) — Krashen
ex: The museum's newest acquisition is a painting from the 1800s.
Our cat's favorite new acquisition is a cardboard box.
The company announced its acquisition of a small tech startup.
Reading widely is one of the best ways to support vocabulary acquisition.
Krashen distinguishes language acquisition, which happens through meaningful input, from conscious learning of grammar rules.

words.en: to imitate someone you admire, trying to equal or surpass them
words.ko: (존경하는 대상을) 본받다, 따라 하다, 필적하려 애쓰다; emulation = 본받음, 경쟁적 모방
words.usage: emulate + person / model / success / system; try / hope / seek to emulate; the emulation of exemplars (virtue ethics); worthy of emulation
words.ety: Latin aemulari (to rival, strive to equal), from aemulus (rivaling); cf. emulation, emulous
words.tip: aemulus = rival → copy your role model as if racing to catch up. ⚠ imitate = neutral copy; mimic = surface copy, sometimes mocking; emulate = copy out of admiration, to equal or surpass.
ex: My nephew emulates his older brother in everything, even the way he walks.
She hoped to emulate her mother's patience with difficult people.
Many countries have tried to emulate Finland's education system.
Children learn virtues partly by emulating adults they admire.
When students see a respected teacher use slurs "jokingly," they may emulate that speech as acceptable.

words.en: teaching that aims to make someone accept beliefs uncritically, without regard to reasons or evidence
words.usage: indoctrinate someone (into / with + belief); indoctrination into + ideology; political / religious indoctrination; slide into indoctrination
words.ety: Latin in- (into) + doctrina (teaching), from docere (to teach); cf. doctrine, doctor, docile
words.tip: in + doctrine = pouring a doctrine IN. Contrast educate (e-ducere), leading OUT.
ex: Teaching about hate speech can slide into indoctrination if students are never invited to weigh the reasons for themselves.

words.en: being answerable to others for one's actions and their results; in education policy, systems that judge schools and teachers by measured outcomes
words.usage: hold someone accountable (for X); be accountable to + people; accountability for + outcomes; test-based / school accountability; an accountability system
words.ety: Latin ad- (to) + computare (to count); cf. account, count, compute
words.tip: Accountable = able to be asked to give an account ("count up" what you did). ⚠ responsibility = duty before acting; accountability = answering for it afterward.
ex: Who should be held accountable for the harm a slur causes in a classroom: the speaker, the school, or both?

words.en: 1) the view that some truths or moral rules hold always and everywhere, without exception; 2) (politics) unlimited rule by one sovereign / absolutist (n./adj.): a person holding such a view; allowing no exceptions
words.ko: 절대주의 (↔ 상대주의 relativism) / absolutist = 절대주의자, 절대주의적인
words.usage: moral absolutism; free speech absolutism / a free speech absolutist; reject absolutism; absolutist claims / an absolutist view / stance on + noun
words.ety: Latin absolutus (loosened, set free, complete), from absolvere; cf. absolute, absolve
words.tip: Absolute = untied from all conditions. An absolutist says "no exceptions, ever." ⚠ Its rival is relativism, not pluralism. -ism → -ist (positivism → positivist). Everyday 'so absolutist' = too black-and-white.
ex:
Free speech absolutism leaves no room to regulate even targeted slurs.

absolutist:
My dad is an absolutist about punctuality: late is late, even by one minute.
She takes an absolutist view on lying; she won't even tell white lies.
Free speech absolutists argue that even offensive speech must be protected.
An absolutist zero-tolerance policy can punish a child who was only defending herself.
Waldron challenges the free speech absolutist by asking what such speech does to the dignity of its targets.

words.en: the belief that God or gods do not exist
words.usage: embrace / reject atheism; theism vs. atheism; an avowed / outspoken atheist; atheistic worldview
words.ety: Greek a- (without) + theos (god) + -ism; cf. theism, theology, monotheism, pantheism
words.tip: a- = without (amoral, apolitical), theos = god (theology) → 'without-god-ism'. ⚠ atheism = believes there is no God; agnosticism = holds we cannot know whether God exists.
ex: My grandfather was a devout Buddhist, but my uncle openly embraced atheism.
She describes herself as an atheist but still celebrates Christmas with her family.
Atheism remains socially stigmatized in some communities.
Public schools may teach about religion and atheism without endorsing either.
The debate between theism and atheism turns on what counts as evidence for God's existence.

words.en: the view that genuine knowledge comes only from observation, experience, and scientific method, not from metaphysics or value claims
words.usage: positivism / logical positivism; a positivist approach / account; critique positivism; positivist assumptions about knowledge
words.ety: Latin positivus (laid down, given), from ponere (to place); cf. posit, position, deposit
