words.tip: Positive here = 'posited, given in experience', not 'optimistic'. Only what's laid before you (observable facts) counts. ⚠ logical positivism = the 1920s–30s Vienna Circle version (meaning = verifiability).
ex: Critics argue that positivism in education research treats test scores as the only real evidence of learning.

words.en: (philosophy) known or justified independently of experience; (general) assumed beforehand without examining evidence
words.ko: 선험적인, 경험에 앞서는; (일반) 증거 없이 미리 정해 둔; a posteriori = 후험적인, 경험에 근거한
words.usage: a priori knowledge / truth / reasoning; know / decide / reject X a priori; an a priori assumption (often critical); a priori vs. a posteriori
words.ety: Latin a priori = 'from what is prior (earlier)'; a posteriori = 'from what comes after'; cf. prior, priority, posterior, postpone
words.tip: a priori = in front of experience (prior); a posteriori = behind experience (post-). An 'a priori assumption' in a paper often signals criticism: decided before looking at the evidence.
ex: You can know a priori that a triangle has three sides; you don't need to measure one.
She rejected the idea a priori, without even looking at the evidence.
Policymakers often make a priori assumptions about what low-income families need.
Researchers should avoid deciding a priori which students will struggle.
Whether a word wounds cannot be settled a priori; it depends on its history and context of use.

words.en: 1) to form an idea of; to imagine or understand something in a certain way; 2) to become pregnant
words.usage: conceive of X as Y; conceive a plan / an idea; be conceived as; it is (in)conceivable that + clause; a conception of + noun
words.ety: Latin con- (together, thoroughly) + capere (to take, seize); -ceive family: conceive, perceive, deceive, receive; nouns shift to -cept- (concept, perception, deception, reception)
words.tip: -ceive = take. con- + take = gather an idea and hold it inside your mind (an idea or a baby: both take shape within). ⚠ Family: conceive (form an idea) / perceive (take in through the senses) / deceive (take the truth away) / receive (take back to yourself).
ex: I can't conceive of living without my cats.
The couple had been trying to conceive for two years.
The plan was conceived over coffee and finished in a week.
Many teachers still conceive of learning as the transfer of information.
Butler conceives of hate speech not as a mere expression of attitude but as an act that wounds.

words.en: epistemic: having to do with knowledge, belief, and justification itself; epistemological: having to do with epistemology, the theory or study of knowledge
words.ko: epistemic 인식적인, 앎에 관한 / epistemological 인식론적인, 인식론의
words.usage: epistemic injustice / authority / humility / standing; epistemological assumptions / debates / framework
words.ety: Greek epistēmē (knowledge, understanding); -logy (study of)
words.tip: ⚠ epistemic = about knowing itself (a knower's credibility); epistemological = about theories of knowing (assumptions, frameworks). Like ethical vs. meta-ethical.
ex: Fricker calls it epistemic injustice when a speaker is disbelieved because of prejudice; the study rests on constructivist epistemological assumptions.

words.en: concerned with how things ought to be, setting standards or values (vs. describing how things are)
words.usage: a normative claim / question / theory / framework; normative vs. descriptive / empirical; normatively loaded
words.ety: Latin norma (a carpenter's square, a rule); cf. norm, normal
words.tip: A norma is a builder's square: the ruler you measure "right" by. ⚠ normative ≠ normal. Descriptive says what is; normative says what ought to be.
ex: Her claim that schools should protect students from slurs is normative, not empirical.

words.en: to become aware of something through the senses; to understand or regard something in a particular way
words.ko: 인식하다, 지각하다, (~로) 여기다; perception = 인식, 지각
words.usage: perceive X as Y; be perceived as + adj/noun; perceive that + clause; public perception of + noun; perceived threat / harm
words.ety: Latin per- (through) + capere (to take); cf. conceive, deceive, receive; perceptible, perceptive
words.tip: per- = through → what comes in THROUGH your eyes and ears. Perception is about how things appear to you, which may differ from how they are. ⚠ conceive = form an idea in the mind; perceive = take in from outside.
ex: Dogs can perceive sounds that humans cannot hear.
She perceived a note of sadness in his voice.
Students who are perceived as troublemakers are disciplined more harshly.
Public perception of the policy changed after the news report.
Whether an utterance is perceived as a threat depends partly on the speaker's social position.

words.en: unwitting: not aware of what one is doing or of its effects; witting: aware, deliberate
words.ko: 자기도 모르는, 무심코 한 / 알면서 하는, 의도적인
words.usage: an unwitting victim / accomplice / agent / participant; unwitting propaganda; unwittingly + verb (unwittingly share); a witting choice / participant (rare; usually deliberate, knowing, conscious)
words.ety: Old English witan (to know); cf. wit, witness, wise, wisdom
words.tip: wit = to know (a witness knows what they saw). witting = knowing; un-witting = not knowing. unwitting is far more common than witting.
words.text: "There is also the unwitting propaganda of the deluded but sincere Sandy Hook Conspiracy Theorist"
ex: unwitting:
She became an unwitting victim of the online scam.
He unwittingly left his keys in the car.
The tourists were unwitting extras in the movie scene.
Many users unwittingly share false news because the headline looks reliable.

Teachers can become unwitting agents of exclusion when they repeat stereotypes without noticing.
witting:
Was that a witting choice, or did it just happen?
Not every falsehood is a lie; a lie is a witting attempt to deceive.
He was a witting accomplice to the fraud.

The investigation asked whether the officials were witting participants.
10. Cassam's point is that propaganda can be witting or unwitting, and either way it serves the same political function.

words.en: to interpret words or actions in a particular way
words.ko: (말·행동을) 해석하다, (~로) 이해하다; misconstrue = 오해하다, 잘못 해석하다
words.usage: construe X as Y; be construed as + noun/adj; broadly / narrowly construed; misconstrue + someone's words / intentions
words.ety: Latin con- (together) + struere (to pile up, build); cf. construct, structure, instruct, misconstrue
words.tip: con + struere = build together → stack up the words to build a meaning. Interpretation is a kind of construction. ⚠ perceive = meaning coming in; conceive = framing a concept; construe = reading the meaning of given words or actions.
ex: Please don't construe my silence as agreement.
Her quick reply was construed as rude, though she was just busy.
The court construed the law narrowly, so the protest was allowed.
A teacher's correction can be construed by a shy student as a personal rejection.
Whether a remark is construed as a joke or a threat often depends on who says it and to whom.

words.en: to place words, ideas, or practices in a new context, which changes their meaning or force
words.usage: recontextualize + term / quotation / slur; recontextualization of X in / into Y; be recontextualized as
words.ety: re- (again) + Latin con- (together) + texere (to weave); cf. text, textile, texture
words.tip: Context = what is woven together with the words. Recontextualizing reweaves them into a new fabric, so they mean something else.
ex: Reclaimed slurs show how a word can be recontextualized to subvert its injurious force.

words.en: 1) (philosophy) the condition of being a subject: a self that experiences, thinks, and acts, and how that self is formed; 2) (everyday) being based on personal feelings or opinions rather than facts
words.usage: the formation / constitution of subjectivity; political / gendered / racialized subjectivity; subjectivity is produced through + discourse / language; subjective (adj.)
words.ety: Latin sub- (under) + iacere (to throw): subiectum, 'what lies underneath'; cf. subject, object, project
words.tip: The subject is what lies underneath and does the experiencing. ⚠ subjectivity in theory (주체성) is NOT a criticism; subjectivity in methods talk (주관성) often is. Butler: we become subjects by being addressed, i.e., subjection = subjectivation.
ex: For Butler, being named, even injuriously, is part of how subjectivity is formed.

words.en: for example
words.usage: X (e.g., A, B), with commas around e.g. in parentheses
words.ety: Latin exempli gratia, "for the sake of example"
words.tip: e.g. = Example Given. ⚠ i.e. = In Essence (that is, in other words).
words.text: "whether, e.g., the pupil is not systematically precluded from asking"
ex: Some speech acts (e.g., slurs) wound by their very utterance.

words.en: to mention or point to something indirectly, without naming it outright
words.ko: 넌지시 언급하다, 암시하다; allusion = 암시, 인유
words.usage: allude to + noun (always with 'to'); allude to X without naming Y; make an allusion to + noun; a passing allusion
words.ety: Latin ad- (toward) + ludere (to play); cf. allusion, delude, illusion, ludicrous, prelude
words.tip: ludere = to play → playfully point toward something instead of saying it straight. Same lud- as delude (already in your bank). ⚠ refer to = mention directly; allude to = mention indirectly. ⚠ allude vs. elude (교묘히 피하다); allusion vs. illusion (착각).
ex: She alluded to a "difficult week" but didn't say what had happened.
He kept alluding to his famous uncle, hoping someone would ask.
The senator alluded to the scandal without naming anyone involved.
The professor alluded to Dewey several times, assuming the students had read him.
Coded hate speech often alludes to a group through dog whistles rather than naming it outright.

words.en: v. (1) to mention; (2) refer to X as Y = to call X 'Y'; (3) (of a word) to mean or denote; (4) to consult/look at a source; (5) refer someone to = to send someone to another person/place for help
words.ko: (1) 언급하다 (2) X를 Y라고 부르다 (3) 가리키다, 지칭하다 (4) 참고하다, 참조하다 (5) (다른 곳으로) 보내다, 소개하다
words.usage: refer to X (never 'refer X'); refer to X as Y; X is referred to as Y (passive); the term X refers to Y; refer to Table 2 / your notes; refer someone to a specialist; spelling: referred, referring (stress on -FER); reference (n.), referent (n.)
words.ety: Latin re- (back) + ferre (to carry); cf. transfer, offer, infer, reference
words.tip: re + fer = carry back: you carry the reader's attention TO something. Think of 'to' as the arrow, so refer always needs 'to.' ⚠ refer to X AS Y: both little words are needed.
ex: In her speech, she referred to her childhood in Busan.
Austin refers to these utterances as 'performatives.'
The term 'hate speech' refers to expression that attacks people based on group identity.
For the full results, refer to Table
My doctor referred me to a specialist.

words.en: genuine, real; sincere, in good faith
words.usage: bona fide + noun (a bona fide expert / student / effort / argument); bona fides (n., credentials: establish one's bona fides)
words.ety: Latin bona (good) + fide (faith); cf. fidelity, confide, infidel
words.tip: In good faith' = the real deal you can trust. A bona fide degree is a real one, not fake. Pronounced BOH-nuh FYE-dee.
words.text: "I have the honour of being described by one eminent (if that's the right word) conspiracy theorist and fellow philosopher as a 'bona fide anti-conspiracy buffoon'."
ex: Is this a bona fide antique or a cheap copy?
Only bona fide students can get the discount.
She made a bona fide effort to fix the problem.
The university checks whether applicants hold bona fide degrees.
Not every critique of free speech is a bona fide argument; some are just insults dressed up as theory.

words.en: (adv.) afterward; at a later time, often as a result of what came before
words.ko: 그 후에, 이후에, 나중에 / subsequent: 뒤이은, 후속의
words.usage: subsequently + verb (was subsequently published / revised); subsequent + noun (subsequent studies / chapters / years); subsequent to X (= after X, formal); in subsequent work
words.ety: Latin sub- 'under, next' + sequi 'to follow' → 'following next.' Same root: sequence, consequence, sequel, consecutive
words.tip: sequ = follow (sequence, sequel) → subsequently = in what followed. Formal version of 'later / afterward.' ⚠ subsequently (그 후에) vs. consequently (그 결과로)
ex: She moved to Chicago in 2020 and subsequently found a job downtown.
The cat ate too fast and was subsequently sick on the rug.
The paper was presented at a conference and subsequently published in a journal.
Subsequent studies failed to replicate the original findings.
Austin's account of speech acts was subsequently developed by Searle and later challenged by Butler.

words.en: hostility toward, prejudice against, or hatred of Jews
words.usage: right-wing / left-wing anti-Semitism; coded anti-Semitism; an anti-Semitic conspiracy theory / slur / trope; advance the cause of anti-Semitism
words.ety: anti- (against) + Semite (from Shem, son of Noah; once used for speakers of Semitic languages); term coined in Germany in 1879 to give Jew-hatred a 'scientific' label
words.tip: Read it as one word meaning hostility toward Jews specifically. There is no separate ideology called 'Semitism'.
words.text: "the point of Conspiracy Theories about the Holocaust is to advance the cause of right-wing anti-Semitism."
ex: The school held a workshop on recognizing anti-Semitism online.
Swastika graffiti on the synagogue was condemned as an act of anti-Semitism.
She wrote her thesis on the history of anti-Semitism in nineteenth-century Europe.
Critics argued that the politician's remarks about "global bankers" were coded anti-Semitism.
Like other forms of hate speech, anti-Semitic slurs can wound through their history of use, not just their literal meaning.

words.en: (Bourdieu) the knowledge, tastes, manners, language and credentials that give a person social advantage, especially in school
words.usage: have / possess / lack cultural capital; accumulate / acquire / transmit cultural capital; cultural capital + translates into / is converted into + noun; cf. economic capital, social capital
words.ety: capital (Latin caput, head → 대표 자산, 밑천) used by Pierre Bourdieu for non-economic resources; three forms: embodied, objectified, institutionalized
words.tip: 돈(economic capital)처럼 '쌓고, 물려주고, 바꿀 수 있는' 문화 → 학교가 보상하는 취향·말투·학벌. 짝꿉 세트: economic / social / cultural capital
ex: Knowing which fork to use at a formal dinner is a small piece of cultural capital.
Her parents took her to museums every weekend, giving her plenty of cultural capital.
Students who lack cultural capital may struggle to read the unspoken rules of a classroom.
Bourdieu argued that schools reward cultural capital while presenting the result as individual merit.
A standard accent can function as cultural capital, while a stigmatized dialect is treated as a deficit.

words.en: to push a person or group to the edge of a society or conversation, treating them as unimportant or powerless
words.usage: marginalize + group / voices; marginalized communities / students; be marginalized by / within + institution
words.ety: Latin margo (edge, border); cf. margin, marginal
words.tip: Picture the margin of a page: what's pushed there is outside the main text. ⚠ Often passive/adjective: marginalized groups.
ex: Curricula that ignore immigrant histories marginalize students from those communities.

words.en: (v.) to get rid of unwanted people or things; to cleanse someone of a bad feeling or impurity. (n.) a sudden removal of opponents from an organization
words.ko: 숙청(하다), 제거하다, 없애다, (마음을) 정화하다 / purgation: 정화, 배설
words.usage: purge A of B (cleanse A by removing B); purge B from A; purge oneself of guilt/fear; a political purge; purgation of emotions (Aristotle's catharsis)
words.ety: Latin purgare 'to make clean' (purus 'pure' + agere 'to make'). Related: pure, purify, purgatory (연옥)
words.tip: purge = make PURE: clear out what's 'dirty' or unwanted. Purgatory is where souls get cleaned. Note the two directions: purge the party OF dissenters = purge dissenters FROM the party
ex: I purged my closet of clothes I haven't worn in years.
She tried to purge the memory from her mind, but it kept coming back.
The new leader purged the party of anyone who disagreed with him.
Some readers interpret Aristotle's catharsis as a purgation of pity and fear.
Attempts to purge classrooms of all offensive language may leave students unprepared to respond to hate speech.

words.en: adj. lower in rank or importance; n. a person under another's authority; v. to place under control or treat as less important
words.ko: adj. 하위의, 종속된; n. 부하; v. 종속시키다, (~보다) 뒤로 두다; subordination = 종속, 예속
words.usage: be subordinate to + noun; subordinate X to Y; one's subordinates; the subordination of + group; speech that subordinates (Langton). Pronunciation: adj./n. -nət, v. -neɪt
words.ety: Latin sub- (under) + ordinare (to arrange, put in order), from ordo (order, rank); cf. order, ordinary, coordinate, insubordinate
words.tip: sub- = under, ordin = order/rank → put someone in a lower slot of the ranking. coordinate = place side by side in the same rank; insubordinate = refusing the lower slot (반항하는).
ex: The manager treats her subordinates with respect.
In the army, a lieutenant is subordinate to a captain.
She subordinated her own career to her children's needs for years.
A curriculum that subordinates students' voices to standardized test scores teaches them that their thinking matters less.
Langton argues that hate speech does not merely express contempt; it subordinates its targets by ranking them as inferior.

words.en: symmetrical: balanced, equal on both sides; asymmetrical: unequal or unbalanced, especially in power or position
words.usage: asymmetrical power relations; an asymmetry of power / between X and Y; the relationship is asymmetrical
words.ety: Greek a- (not) + syn- (together) + metron (measure); cf. meter, geometry
words.tip: sym-metry = same measure on both sides. A-symmetry: one side weighs more. In critical theory it almost always means power imbalance.
ex: A slur from a teacher to a student wounds differently because the relationship is asymmetrical.

words.en: organized action to bring about social or political change
words.usage: engage in activism; student / grassroots / anti-racist activism; scholar-activist; activism and scholarship
words.ety: Latin agere / actus (to do, act); cf. action, agent, active
words.tip: Activism = action aimed at change, not just study. ⚠ activist research = scholarship tied to that goal.
ex: Some philosophers worry that activism compromises the neutrality of scholarship.

words.en: a principle, aim, or movement that people support and work for (not 'reason' here)
words.usage: advance / further / promote a cause; support / champion / fight for / take up a cause; the cause of X (the cause of children's rights); a good cause; a lost cause; political causes
words.ety: Latin causa: 1) reason → cause (원인), because; 2) lawsuit, case in court → the side you plead for → a principle you fight for; cf. excuse, accuse
words.tip: From the courtroom: you plead someone's cause = take their side. Today's 'cause' = the side you push forward. Tell them apart: cause OF + result = 원인; ADVANCE / SUPPORT + cause = 대의.
words.text: "Conspiracy Theories are part of a conspiracy to advance right-wing political causes." / "to advance the cause of right-wing anti-Semitism"
ex: She has devoted her life to the cause of children's rights.
The concert raised money for a good cause.
Trying to change his mind is a lost cause.
Many students joined the cause after the protest.
Hate speech is often defended in the name of free speech, even when it advances causes that silence others.

words.en: (n.) a wide gap or difference between people, groups, or ideas; (literal) a large bay of sea
words.ko: (생각·입장 사이의) 큰 격차, 간극, 단절; 만(灣)
words.usage: a gulf between A and B; a widening/growing gulf; bridge the gulf (간극을 잇다/메우다); a gulf separates A from B; the Gulf of Mexico
words.ety: Greek kolpos 'bosom, bay' → Italian golfo → French golfe. Related: engulf (삼키다, 휩쓸다)
words.tip: Picture the Gulf of Mexico: a huge stretch of water between two shores → a gulf between two people is a wide space they can't easily cross. Stronger than 'gap'; close to 'chasm', 'divide'
ex: There's a wide gulf between what he says and what he does.
After the argument, a gulf opened up between the two sisters.
The gulf between rich and poor neighborhoods keeps widening.
Good teachers try to bridge the gulf between theory and classroom practice.
Austin's distinction exposes a gulf between what a speaker means and what a word does to its target.

words.en: bitter, ongoing conflict or struggle between people or groups; discord, often with a sense of unrest that runs deep
words.usage: civil / social / political / ethnic / religious strife; internal strife; marital / family strife; be torn apart / riven by strife; a source of strife; stir up / sow strife; a time of strife
words.ety: Old French estrif (quarrel, dispute) from estriver (to strive); related to Germanic roots; cf. strive
words.tip: strife = what you get when people strive against each other: strive (verb) → strife (noun). Broader and more literary than 'fight'; it names the lasting state of conflict, not a single quarrel.
ex: Years of civil strife drove thousands of families to leave the country.
Money was a constant source of strife in their marriage.
The new policy stirred up strife among the teachers.
The school, torn by racial strife, struggled to teach students to listen to one another.
Hobbes pictured life without a sovereign as a state of constant strife, a 'war of all against all'.

words.en: n. open, bold refusal to obey or respect authority, a rule, or an opponent; v. defy = to openly resist; also to resist explanation (defy description / logic / the odds)
words.ko: n. (공공연한) 반항, 저항, 도전 / v. 거역하다, 맞서다; (설명·예상 등을) 무색하게 하다
words.usage: in defiance of + law / order / rules; an act / gesture of defiance; open / quiet defiance; defy authority / the odds / description; defiant (adj.), defiantly (adv.) ⚠ vs. resistance: defiance is open and bold, often provocative; resistance can be quiet or structural
words.ety: Old French defier (to challenge, renounce allegiance), from de- (away, un-) + fier (to trust), Latin fidus (faithful); cf. fidelity, confide, fiancé
words.tip: de + fi(des) = un-faith: you withdraw your loyalty and openly say "No." Same 'fi' as fidelity (faithfulness), so defiance is the opposite of obedient fidelity.
ex: The toddler shook her head in defiance when told to go to bed.
He kept smoking on the balcony in open defiance of the building rules.
Wearing black to the ceremony was a small act of defiance.
Rosa Parks's refusal to give up her seat became a lasting symbol of defiance against segregation laws.
Reclaiming a slur can be read as an act of defiance: the targeted group turns the wounding word against the authority that coined it.

words.en: information, often biased or misleading, spread to shape people's beliefs and actions in favor of a political cause
words.usage: political / wartime / state / hate propaganda; a piece of propaganda; spread / produce / peddle propaganda; dismiss X as propaganda; sincere / unwitting propaganda (Stanley, Cassam)
words.ety: Latin propagare (to spread, multiply); from Congregatio de Propaganda Fide (1622, Catholic body 'for spreading the faith'); turned negative after WWI and WWII; cf. propagate
words.tip: Originally just 'spreading the faith' (neutral). Today: spreading beliefs to steer people, bypassing their judgment. ⚠ persuasion = giving reasons (neutral or good); propaganda = manipulating for a political end; indoctrination = in the guise of education.
words.text: "Conspiracy Theories are first and foremost forms of political propaganda."
ex: The poster was wartime propaganda urging citizens to hate the enemy.
The state-run TV channel broadcasts government propaganda every night.
Critics dismissed the documentary as pure propaganda.
Social media bots spread propaganda faster than fact-checkers can respond.
Hate propaganda often works by portraying a minority group as a threat to "us."

words.en: firm determination; the quality of having decided and holding to it without wavering
words.usage: act / face X with resoluteness; resoluteness in the face of + difficulty; be resolute in doing / in one's commitment; resolutely refuse / defend
words.ety: Latin resolvere (to loosen, settle), re- + solvere (to untie); cf. resolve, resolution, solve
words.tip: Once a question is resolved (settled), you stop wavering. ⚠ In Heidegger, resoluteness (Entschlossenheit) is a technical term: owning one's situation and choices authentically.
ex: After the setback, she faced the next round of interviews with quiet resoluteness.
His resoluteness in refusing the bribe earned him the town's respect.
The coach admired the team's resoluteness in the face of a brutal schedule.
Teachers who interrupt a slur in class need resoluteness, not just good intentions.
In Heidegger, resoluteness (Entschlossenheit) means owning one's situation and choices authentically.

words.en: holding on firmly and persistently, refusing to let go or give up
words.usage: cling / hold on / defend + tenaciously; a tenacious belief / myth / stereotype; tenacity (n.); with tenacity
words.ety: Latin tenere (to hold); cf. tenant, tenet, retain, maintain
words.tip: Same root as tenant (one who holds a place) and tenet (a belief one holds): tenacious = keeps holding. ⚠ Can be praise (a tenacious researcher) or negative (a stereotype that persists tenaciously).
ex: Stereotypes embedded in slurs persist tenaciously even after the words themselves fall out of use.

words.en: 1) unusual, odd behavior or habits that depart from what is conventional (usually harmless, even charming); 2) an odd habit itself (countable: eccentricities); 3) (math/astronomy) how far an orbit or curve departs from a perfect circle
words.ko: 1) 별남, 기이함, 괴짜 기질; 2) 기벽, 별난 버릇; 3) (수학·천문) 이심률
words.usage: the eccentricity of + person / style; an eccentricity (= one odd habit); harmless / charming eccentricities; tolerate / indulge someone's eccentricities; eccentric (adj./n.): an eccentric professor; eccentrically
words.ety: Greek ek- (out of) + kentron (center; originally the sharp point of a compass); cf. center, concentric, egocentric, ethnocentric
words.tip: ec-centric = off-center: someone whose life doesn't circle the usual center. ⚠ vs. idiosyncratic: idiosyncratic = peculiar to one person (often about a view or style); eccentric = noticeably odd behavior, usually harmless. vs. eccentricity as orbit term = how off-center an orbit is.
ex: His only eccentricity was wearing a bow tie to the gym.
The town tolerated the old painter's eccentricities: the purple house, the parrot on his shoulder.
Earth's orbit has low eccentricity, so it is close to a circle.
What one culture calls eccentricity, another may see as perfectly ordinary behavior.
Mill defended eccentricity as a safeguard against the 'tyranny of the majority' in On Liberty.

words.en: peculiar to one individual; unusual and personal rather than shared or standard
words.usage: an idiosyncratic reading / style / view / use of a term; idiosyncrasy (n.); highly idiosyncratic
words.ety: Greek idios (one's own, private) + syn- (together) + krasis (mixture); cf. idiom, idiot (orig. 'private person')
words.tip: idio- = one's own (idiom = a language's own expression). Your own personal mix. ⚠ In academic writing it can be mildly critical: 'not generalizable, just this author's quirk.'
ex: He has an idiosyncratic way of organizing his books: he sorts them by color rather than by author.
Her handwriting is so idiosyncratic that only her close friends can read it.
The film's idiosyncratic style, with long silences and odd camera angles, isn't for everyone.
Rawls uses 'justice' in a fairly standard way, but Derrida's use of the term is highly idiosyncratic.
The reviewer called the author's reading of Austin idiosyncratic: it reflects the author's own take and wouldn't be widely accepted.

words.en: (of a person, idea, or device) clever, original, and inventive
words.usage: an ingenious solution / argument / device / way of doing X; ingenuity (n.); ingeniously argue / combine
words.ety: Latin ingenium (natural talent, inborn cleverness), in- + gignere (to beget); cf. engine, engineer, genius
words.tip: Same root as engine / engineer: an ingenious idea is one an engineer would admire. ⚠ ingenuous = naive, innocent (in-genuous = genuine, no tricks).
ex: Langton offers an ingenious way to apply Austin's speech act theory to pornography.

words.en: (idiom) a very shy, timid person who avoids attention
words.ko: 수줍음 많은 사람, 나서지 않는 사람
words.usage: mostly negative: not exactly / hardly / no shrinking violet (= bold, outspoken); be a shrinking violet
words.ety: shrink (to draw back, cower) + violet (a small flower growing low, half-hidden in grass); idiom from the early 19th century
words.tip: A tiny violet hiding low in the grass and pulling back from view. Usually ironic: 'not exactly a shrinking violet' = loud, pushy, unafraid.
words.text: "perhaps it's worth remembering that they aren't exactly shrinking violets. They are vociferous defenders of their theories"
ex: My little sister is no shrinking violet; she'll talk to anyone.
He was a shrinking violet at parties but confident in the lab.
You can't be a shrinking violet if you want to sell your ideas to investors.
At the faculty meeting, she was hardly a shrinking violet; she challenged the dean twice.
Critics of the policy are not exactly shrinking violets; they have filled the comment section with angry replies.

words.en: a ridiculous fool; a clown who makes people laugh, often unintentionally
words.ko: 어릿광대, 바보 같은 사람 / 얼간이 짓
words.usage: act like / play the buffoon; dismiss someone as a buffoon; a pompous buffoon; political buffoonery
words.ety: Italian buffone (jester), from buffa (joke, puff of the cheeks); cf. opera buffa (comic opera), buffo
words.tip: Buffoon makes buffa (jokes): picture a clown in a comic opera. Fetzer calls Cassam a 'bona fide anti-conspiracy buffoon' = a genuine clown who blindly opposes conspiracy theories.
words.text: "described ... as a 'bona fide anti-conspiracy buffoon'"
ex: He acted like a buffoon at the wedding and embarrassed everyone.
The cartoon shows the king as a pompous buffoon.
Stop playing the buffoon and take this seriously.
Critics dismissed the politician as a buffoon, but he won anyway.
Calling an opponent a buffoon is an ad hominem move: it mocks the person instead of answering the argument.

words.en: done openly and obviously, without trying to hide it (usually about something bad)
words.usage: a blatant lie / disregard / foul / violation / discrimination; a blatant example / piece of X; blatantly false / obvious; opp. subtle, covert
words.ety: Coined by Edmund Spenser (1596) for the noisy 'Blatant Beast'; possibly from Latin blatire (to babble)
words.tip: A loud, in-your-face beast: the wrongdoing isn't hidden, it's shouting at you. ⚠ blatant (shameless, not even trying to hide) vs. flagrant (obvious and serious, often a rule-breaking).
words.text: "the Sandy Hook conspiracy theory is a blatant piece of political propaganda" / "a blatant example of fake news"
ex: That's a blatant lie; I saw you take the cookie.
The referee ignored a blatant foul right in front of him.
The company showed a blatant disregard for worker safety.
The essay was rejected for blatant plagiarism.
Some slurs are blatant, while other forms of hate speech work through subtle, coded language.

words.en: extremely cruel or wicked; cleverly evil (of a plan); (informal) very difficult or clever
words.ko: 악마 같은, 극악무도한; 교활하고 사악한; (구어) 엄청나게 어려운
words.usage: a fiendish plot / scheme / plan / trick; fiendishly difficult / clever / complex; fiend (n.) = demon, or informal 'fan, addict' (a coffee fiend)
words.ety: fiend (demon) + -ish; Old English fēond (enemy); cf. German Feind (enemy)
words.tip: fiend = demon → fiendish = demon-like: the cartoon villain's evil master plan. ⚠ 'fiendishly difficult' = just very hard (not evil).
words.text: "a member of a group of Jewish elders outlines a fiendish plot for world domination"
ex: The villain in the movie had a fiendish plan to poison the city's water.
The puzzle was fiendishly difficult; nobody solved it in an hour.
The prisoners were subjected to fiendish tortures.
She came up with a fiendish trick to make her brother do the dishes.
Anti-Semitic propaganda has long portrayed Jews as masterminds of a fiendish plot to control the world.

words.en: to allow yourself or someone else to have or do something enjoyable, often without restraint
words.ko: (욕구를) 마음껏 채우다, 탐닉하다; (남의 바람을) 너그럽게 들어주다, 응석을 받아 주다; indulgence = 탐닉, 관대, 면죄부; self-indulgent = 자기만족적인
words.usage: indulge in + noun (chocolate / speculation / nostalgia); indulge + person (a child); indulge someone's wish / whim; Indulge me (for a moment); self-indulgent writing
words.ety: Latin indulgere (to be kind, yield, grant); cf. indulgent, indulgence (historical: 면죄부)
words.tip: indulgere = be lenient → 'just this once, go ahead.' indulgence = the medieval pardon that let sins slide. ⚠ Academic use is often critical: indulge in speculation, self-indulgent prose.
ex: On Fridays I indulge in a big bowl of ice cream.
Grandparents often indulge their grandchildren with sweets and toys.
Please indulge me for a moment; I want to tell you a short story.
Teachers who indulge every off-topic question may lose the thread of the lesson.
To dismiss victims' pain as "oversensitivity" is to indulge the speaker's comfort at the target's expense.

words.en: inspiring fear or awe because of great power, size, or ability
words.usage: a formidable figure / opponent / critic / task / challenge / presence; formidably (adv.)
words.ety: Latin formidabilis, from formido (fear, dread); cf. formidably
words.tip: formido = fear. Something formidable makes you a little afraid at first, then impressed. Often a compliment: 'a formidable scholar' = impressively capable.
words.text: "Freud presents himself as such a formidable figure that it may at first be difficult to imagine him creating an atmosphere in which it is sufficiently safe for the patient..."
words.source: Lear, Love and Its Place in Nature, Ch. 2, p. 59
ex: The mountain looked formidable from the bottom, but the trail was easier than we expected.
She's a formidable chess player; I've never beaten her.
Learning a new language as an adult is a formidable task.
Butler is a formidable critic of the view that speech simply reflects existing power.
Freud's formidable presence may have made it hard for patients to speak freely.

words.en: no longer used or useful because something newer has replaced it; out of date to the point of being abandoned
words.ko: 더 이상 쓰이지 않는, 시대에 뒤떨어진, 구식의, 폐기된
words.usage: become obsolete; render / make X obsolete; be rendered obsolete by Y; obsolete technology / word / law / method / assumption; obsolescence (n.); planned obsolescence
words.ety: Latin obsolescere (to fall into disuse), from ob- (away) + solere (to be accustomed); cf. insolent (originally 'unaccustomed')
words.tip: ob- (away) + solere (be accustomed): no longer what people are accustomed to using. Stronger than 'outdated': obsolete means the field has moved on, not just that the thing is old.
ex: Floppy disks became obsolete once USB drives and cloud storage took over.
The word 'thou' is obsolete in everyday English, though you still see it in old texts.
The new software rendered our old workflow obsolete overnight.
Critics argue that standardized testing is an obsolete way to measure what students actually understand.
Calling a theory obsolete is stronger than calling it wrong: it implies that the field has simply moved on.

words.en: to become progressively worse over time
words.ko: 악화되다, 나빠지다; deterioration = 악화 (↔ ameliorate 개선하다)
words.usage: X deteriorates; deteriorate rapidly / steadily / sharply; deteriorate into + worse state; the deterioration of/in + noun
words.ety: Latin deterior (worse), comparative form related to de- (down); cf. deteriorative; opposite: ameliorate (from melior, better)
words.tip: de- = down, deterior = worse → going down step by step, getting worse and worse. Pair it with its opposite ameliorate (melior = better).
ex: The old wooden fence has deteriorated badly over the years.
His health deteriorated quickly after the surgery.
Relations between the two countries deteriorated after the trade dispute.
Teachers warn that classroom discussion deteriorates when students feel unsafe to speak.
Repeated exposure to slurs can cause a group's sense of standing in the community to deteriorate.

words.en: to make something bad or unsatisfactory better; to lessen a problem
words.ko: 개선하다, (나쁜 상황을) 완화하다; amelioration = 개선, 완화 (↔ deteriorate 악화되다)
words.usage: ameliorate + problem / conditions / effects / harm / suffering; ameliorate but not eliminate; efforts to ameliorate + noun; the amelioration of + noun
words.ety: Latin ad- (toward) + melior (better), via French améliorer; cf. meliorism (belief that the world can be improved); opposite: deteriorate (from deterior, worse)
words.tip: melior = better → a + melior = move toward better. Pair with deteriorate: deterior (worse) ↘ / melior (better) ↗. Nuance: it eases something already bad rather than removing it.
ex: A cup of warm tea ameliorated my sore throat a little.
The city built more shelters to ameliorate conditions for the homeless in winter.
Free school meals can ameliorate, but not eliminate, the effects of poverty on learning.
Policies that only ameliorate symptoms may leave the underlying injustice untouched.
Counter-speech may ameliorate the harm of a slur, but it cannot undo the wound entirely.

words.en: to make something bad less severe, harmful, or painful
words.usage: mitigate + harm/risk/effects/damage/impact; mitigate the effects of X; mitigation strategies; mitigating circumstances (정상참작의 사유)
words.ety: Latin mitis 'soft, mild' + agere 'to make' → 'make milder'. Related: (un)mitigated (an unmitigated disaster = 완전한 재앙)
words.tip: mit = mild → mitigate = make the bad thing milder (it doesn't remove it). ⚠ mitigate (완화하다) vs. militate against (~에 불리하게 작용하다). Compare ameliorate (make a bad situation better)
ex: Drinking water can help mitigate a headache.
Planting trees helps mitigate the effects of summer heat in cities.
The judge considered his young age a mitigating circumstance.
Schools adopted new policies to mitigate the risk of bullying online.
Counter-speech may mitigate, but not fully undo, the harm of a racial slur.

words.en: just beginning to exist or develop; still in an early, not fully formed stage
words.usage: nascent + noun (a nascent movement / field / industry / democracy / idea); in its nascent stage; still nascent
words.ety: Latin nasci 'to be born' → nascens 'being born'. Same root: native, nation, nature, prenatal, Renaissance ('re-birth')
words.tip: nasc = born (native, Renaissance) → nascent = 'still being born,' not grown up yet. Compare primordial (맨 처음의, existing from the very start)
ex: Our nascent friendship grew stronger after the trip.
The startup is still nascent, with only three employees.
Her nascent interest in painting turned into a lifelong hobby.
In the 1990s, the internet was a nascent technology.
Students' nascent understanding of injustice can be nurtured through careful classroom discussion.

words.en: existing from the very beginning; most basic and fundamental
words.usage: primordial + noun (soup / forest / fear / instinct / desire / unity); primordial in + noun; (philosophy) the primordial = what comes first, before anything else
words.ety: Latin primordium (the very beginning) = primus (first) + ordiri (to begin, to lay the first threads of a weave); cf. primary, prime, primitive, primeval
words.tip: primus (first) + ordiri (start weaving) → the very first thread of the cloth: what comes before everything else. ⚠ Spelling: pri-MORD-ial (not 'primodial'). ⚠ primordial vs. primitive: primordial = 'first / most basic' (neutral or deep); primitive = 'undeveloped, crude' (often negative).
ex: Some scientists believe life began in a primordial soup of chemicals.
The hikers walked through a primordial forest that had never been logged.
A baby's fear of falling seems almost primordial.
For many myths, the world begins in primordial darkness and chaos.
Some philosophers treat our openness to others as primordial, prior to any social rule or contract.

words.en: a sudden, violent, or major change that disrupts a situation, society, or someone's life
words.usage: (a) social/political/emotional upheaval; personal upheaval; cause/bring upheaval; go through/undergo an upheaval; a period/time of upheaval; upheavals in + area (upheavals in education)
words.ety: up + heave 'lift with effort' → the ground literally heaved up (originally of earthquakes). Related: heave (들어 올리다, 기복)
words.tip: Picture an earthquake heaving the ground UP → everything that was stable gets turned over. Stronger than 'change'; close to 'turmoil', 'disruption'
ex: Moving to a new country was a huge upheaval for the whole family.
The kids needed time to adjust after the upheaval of changing schools.
The pandemic caused major upheavals in how people work.
Periods of political upheaval often lead to sweeping changes in school curricula.
For Freud, early emotional upheavals leave traces that shape how a person later relates to the world.
